California Masonic Memorial Temple - San Francisco

MELVILLE H. NAHIN

Grand Master 1998-1999
Our Grand Master was born in Chicago, Illinois, on July 19, 1929, moved to
California at an early age, and attended the Los Angeles public schools. He graduated from
the University of California, Los Angeles, and received a Juris Doctor degree from the
Loyola University Law School. He has been engaged in the practice of law since 1953.
Our Grand Master has been married forty-nine years to his wife Alice, and they
have two sons, Richard, a research scientist, and Bruce, an attorney and partner with his
father in the law firm of Nahin and Nahin. Bruce and his wife Debi have two children,
Jacob and Nicolas.
Our Grand Master became a Master Mason in Ionic Lodge No. 520, and served
his Lodge as Master in 1966. The Lodge honored him by naming him the first recipient of
the Isadore Moore Masonic Service Award in 1972, and the Vierling Kersey Award for
Outstanding Contributions to Youth in 1981. He received the Hiram Award in 1995. He is
a noted Masonic author contributing regularly to the Scottish Rite Journal, the California
Freemason, and the Indiana Freemason. He is a member of the Stephen S. Wise Temple
in Los Angeles, where he has served on the Budget and Finance Committee, and the Ways
and Means Committee.
Because of the importance Brother Nahin places on our youth, he has devoted
time and effort in supporting the Order of DeMolay. He served as the Chairman of the
Executive Committee for the Order of DeMolay, Southern Jurisdiction, as well as serving
as their legal counsel for 25 years. His DeMolay honors include the DeMolay Legion of
Honor, the DeMolay Cross of Honor, and he has been awarded the "Guild of the Leather
Apron" as the outstanding Advisor in Southern California Jurisdiction. He currently serves
as a Deputy Member of the Supreme Council of DeMolay International.

.

He served as Venerable Master of the Los Angeles Lodge of Perfection in 1984.
He served for 14 years as the Chairman of the Childhood Language Disorders Clinic, and
for 12 years as the Vice President of the California Scottish Rite Foundation. He was
coroneted in 1981 with the Thirty-Third Degree, Honorary, by the Supreme Council, A.&
A.S.R., Southern Jurisdiction. He served for 12 years as a member of the Board of
Governors of the Los Angeles Shriners Hospital for Children and for two years as
Chairman of the Board.

MELVILLE H. NAHIN
Grand Master
October 14, 1998 - October 13, 1999

ii

Most Worshipful Brother Nahin has served the Grand Lodge of California in
many capacities over the years, including the Special Committee on Code Revision, which
produced the current California Masonic Code. He served as Chairman of both the
Jurisprudence Committee and the Committee on Trial Review. In 1979 Past Grand Master
Donald Ingalls appointed him to the Special Commission to Study the Structure of Grand
Lodge. In 1981 he was appointed as Grand Orator by Past Grand Master Robert West.
Brother Nahin has also served as a member of the Boards of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes of California, California Masonic Foundation, the California Masonic Memorial
Temple, and the Nob Hill Masonic Management Corporation.

PUBLIC OPENIN G CEREMO NY
Sunday, October 10, 1999
2:30 PM

The Public Opening of Grand Lodge was held in the Masonic Auditorium
ofthe California Masonic Memorial Temple, 1111 California Street, San Francisco,
California, beginning at 2:30 p.m. Grand Master Melville H. Nahin, accompanied
by his Grand Lodge Officers, entered the Auditorium to the sound of trumpets and
organ, and assumed their stations. The Grand Chaplain gave the invocation.
The Grand Master thanked Mrs. Sheri Weisser, Worthy Grand Matron,
Grand Chapter ofCalifornia, Order ofthe Eastern Star, for raising the Grand Lodge.
He noted that this is a "first" for the Grand Lodge of California, and that we could
not have chosen a better representative of the Family of Freemasonry than Sheri.
He expressed his appreciation that she was willing to honor us with her presence
today.
The Grand Master then announced that the following gavels had been used
by the Worthy Grand Matron to raise the Grand Lodge: First, a commemorative
gavel used on June 6, 1999, when Grand Lodge laid the cornerstone for the Eastern
Star Senior Living Community at Yorba Linda; second, a carved wooden gavel in
the form of a "lobster," with a "shell" sounding block, made by Cole and Joanne
Lipking, the aunt and uncle of Vicki Foran, wife of our Grand Chaplain, Sean
Foran, and presented at the New England Summer Picnic on July 10, 1999,
sponsored by the Ventura Scottish Rite; third, a wooden gavel from Israel,
presented on May 17, 1999 by Worshipful Brother Wayne Butterbaugh on the
occasion of the Grand Master's trip to Israel in May; and fourth, a gavel with a
wood burl soundiJlg block, presented on June 16, 1999, at the 3051h Masonic
District Reception for the Grand Master at Victorville.
The Grand Master then directed the Grand Marshal to retire and present
the Flag of our Country before the Altar of Freemasonry.
The Grand Master invited the Brethren and ladies to join with him in the
Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag of Our Country. He then delivered a stirring
Tribute to the Flag. The Flag Tribute, in its entirety, can be found in Appendix A
of these Proceedings.
The Grand Master noted that the Flag of the United States of America
which was escorted by the Grand Marshal had been presented to him at a reception
of the Valley of Santa Ana Scottish Rite on September 13, 1999 and had been flown
over the Battleship U.S.S. Arizona on July 19, 1999, and thereafter flown over the
U.S.S. Missouri on September 2, 1999, the anniversary of the peace accord that was
signed on the U.S.S. Missouri, attesting to the surrender of the Japanese military
and ending World War II on that same date 54 years before.
The Grand Master reminded those assembled in the California Masonic
Memorial Temple, which has been designated as a war memorial building, that in
this era of peace we enjoy our American freedoms, among which are the right
peaceably to assemble and to speak our minds as we see fit to do so. He
emphasized that we should never forget the price that many of our fellow
Americans paid for these freedoms and continue to do so in defense of our
American freedoms.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

RESPONS E TO THE WELCOM E TO DISTINGUISHED VISITORS
By M :.W:. H. Douglas Lemons, P.G.M.
Sovereign Grand Inspector General in California
Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry, S.J.

At the conclusion of his remarks, Brother Lemons presented a check in
the amount of$10,000 for the Tournamen t of Roses Parade Float.
The Grand Marshal was called upon to retire and escort into Grand Lodge
the visitors from our sister Grand Lodges, and there were presented for
introduction:

Most Worshipful Melville H. Nahin, Grand lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters,
My Brethren and Distinguished Guests:
On behalf of all the distinguished visitors graciously welcomed this
afternoon by the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California, I wish to thank you
all for your courtesy and your kind and considerate demonstration of cordiality.
Each of the organizations we represent recognizes the Grand Lodge as the cradle
for all Masonry in California. You are our parents-o ur Mother and our Father-and on this occasion we proudly return home to pay homage to and be welcomed
by those from whence we came.
Most Worshipful Sir, you and I are hardly strangers; we have on many
occasions and over a long period of time worked shoulder to shoulder in the
vineyards of Freemasonry. But on this occasion I rise to honor your efforts and
your accomplishments on behalf of our great Fraternity through your office of Most
Worshipful Grand Master. You have as no one before you elevated the visibility
of our Craft to a height never before dreamed possible. Several of us here this
afternoon represent concordant and appendant bodies of the Family ofFreemas onry
who have joined you financially in supporting the new Grand Lodge Public
Relations Program. Thank you for allowing us to join you in your dreams.
Watching many of these dreams become reality has been our reward.
I join everyone in this beautiful building in wishing you and the lovely
lady Alice the very finest life has to offer, as you leave your distinguished and Most
Worshipful station in the East. May we, your guests, take this opportunity to
pledge our allegiance to and pledge our support for this Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge. We pledge to re-double our efforts on behalf of membership, camaraderie
and the strength of the Order.
We are proud to be a part of the oldest and finest Fraternity in the world
and join hands with you in reaching outto humanity and together may we touch and
heal broken hearts and bodies. May we together live the philosophies and ideals
of our calling with such effectiveness that we together might be as a banner and an
ensign to this great nation called America, as well as to free people all throughout
the world, and those who would be free be in every continent around the world.
Thank you for your thoughtful and gracious hospitality.

The Grand Master welcomed the leaders of the Masonic youth groups,
expressing the thanks of the Masonic Fraternity fortheir dedication and leadership.
He then asked the Grand Marshal to conduct the adult leaders of our Masonic
Youth Groups to seats in the auditorium, and then conduct the elected leaders to
seats in the East.
The Grand Master then presented the Grand Master's Youth Achievement
Award for 1999. This year there were four recipients who have been selected to
receive the award. Brother Raymond Peltier, Chairman of the Grand Lodge Youth
Orders Committee, assisted the Grand Master in presenting the award to the
recipients by reading a brief biography of each honoree. At the direction of the
Grand Master, the Grand Marshal escorted Brother Bryan Frymire; Worshipful
Glen Thurber; Brother Arthur Calloway; and Worshipful Donald Stephens, to a
place West of the Altar. The Grand Master, joined by the Deputy Grand Master,
presented each Brother with the award and medallion. The Grand Master then
called on Master Masons in the auditorium to rise and join in giving the four
distinguished Masons the Public Grand Honors of Masonry by Three Times Three.
The Grand Marshal then conducted the brethren to seats in the auditorium.
The Grand Master then called on each of the elected leaders of the
Masonic Youth Groups fora few words. Each spoke eloquently to the assembled
guests, and their remarks were warmly received. After their remarks, the Grand
Master commented that each year the California Masonic Foundation and the Grand
Lodge of California express their support for the Masonic Youth Groups by
financially supporting their leadership training programs. He then presented checks
totaling $4,000 for each of the youth groups-$2,500 from the California Masonic
Foundation and $1,500 from the Grand Lodge of California.
The Grand Master then announced that during the past year he had
approved the organization of a Masonic club which will ultimately lead to the
formation of another research lodge in California. He then called Worshipful
Brother Douglas Cairns, Inspector of the 293'd Masonic District, to the lectern to
receive on behalfofthe Masonic Club the "Letters Temporary" which the Grand
Master had issued to the Masonic Origins Research Club of Fresno, representing
the authority of the Club to form and to meet, with the expectation that they will be
instituted on November 15, 1999, as the Masonic Origins Research Lodge UD.
Brother Cairns received the "Letters Temporary" with thanks and appreciation to
the Grand Master and the Grand Secretary, noting that the leadership of the
Research Lodge is driven by a group of young men under 30 years old, who "are

to have the opportunity to speak with you today about my university experience and

what I have done and so much of what I aspire to accomplish.
I am a third year student at UCLA, majoring in International Relations and
minoring in Mathematics. While in high school, I aimed to excel academically and
was highly involved in extracurricular activities because that is what I enjoyed and
derived a great sense of purpose in doing. I had in mind from grade school just how
I wanted to study for an undergrad degree on the west coast and graduate degree on
the east, but because of my modest financial background, I didn't know just how
it was going to work out, and financing my college education was frankly a great
source of anxiety for me. Then, in my senior year, I received a fateful phone call
from the Masonic Foundation for an interview with Dr. Don Nielsen and Dr.
Wayne Butterbaugh and, as they say, the rest is history ...

much has happened in my life since then, and I have learned and grown such a great

DEVOTIONAL SERVICE
The Grand Lodge Devotional Service was held in the Auditorium of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple, at 4:30 PM. The Invocation was led by the
Grand Chaplain, Very Reverend Sean Foran.
The Grand Master then remarked that the Devotional Service is a
traditional part of the beginning of each Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of California. All Masons must acknowledge a belief in God, whether they
refer to Him as Adonai, Allah, Christ, or any other Name, when first they enter our
doors, and throughout life, all Freemasons acknowledge a dependence upon the
Great Architect of the Universe for His sustaining presence in our lives. It is
therefore appropriate that the Public Opening of Grand Lodge today end with a
sharing together of this acknowledgment of our dependence upon God, and our
thanksgiving for His presence among us over the next few days.

Grand Master's Message
The Grand Master then relinquished his chair to the Deputy Grand Master
for the purpose of delivering the Grand Master's Message (Appendix A). After his
message, the Grand Master received a standing ovation, following which he
resumed his station.
The Grand Master announced that it was now time for consideration of the
legislation before the Grand Lodge. He reminded the Brethren that there were six
Grand Master's Recommendations, four carry-over items, and 29 new resolutions
to consider on Monday and Tuesday. He therefore called upon the Chairman of the
Jurisprudence Committee, Most Worshipful R. Stephen Doan, who presented a
motion to allow him to introduce an emergent resolution, which was seconded by
the Deputy Grand Master, and was passed by the required 5/6 vote of the Grand
Lodge.
Brother Doan then moved that the rules of procedure in Part V of the
California Masonic Code be modified for this Annual Communication only, as
follows: all speakers from the floor, including the proponent, shall be allotted three
minutes each. Only two speakers on each side of an issue, including the proponent,

19

shall be permitted under each item under discussion. The motion was seconded by
the Deputy Grand Master, and was passed by the required 5/6 vote of the Grand
Lodge.
Before breaking for lunch, the Grand Master reviewed the rules that will
govern the handling of all the legislative business and balloting procedures for the
Monday afternoon session and the Tuesday morning session.

At 4:45 p.m. the Grand Master called Grand Lodge from labor to
refreshment, to be called on again at 9:00 a.m. on Tuesday, October 12.

27

TUESDAY MORNING, OCTOBER 12, 1999
Grand Lodge was called on promptly at 9:00 a.m. by Grand Master
Melville M. Nahin and the Grand Chaplain offered prayer. The Grand Master
announced that Grand Lodge had been raised this morning by Worshipful Brother
Bruce Pruitt. The Grand Master expressed his appreciation for Brother Pruitt's five
years of leadership and devoted service as the Chairman of the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board.
The Grand Master announced that this session was raised with the
following gavels: first, a carved wooden gavel with a "mouse" sounding block,
presented to the Grand Master on February 11, 1999, on the occasion of his
Reception at Poinsettia Lodge No. 633, in Ventura; secondly, a commemorative
gavel and sounding block, handcrafted by Worshipful Brother Glenn C. Johnson II,
Past Master and Secretary of San Dimas Lodge No. 448, with the border designed
by Worshipful Brother Gene Bowman, Inspector of the 440th Masonic District. It
was presented on November 20, 1998, on the occasion of a Grand Master's
Reception hosted by the 440th and 441" Masonic Districts in Pomona. Thirdly, a
"setting maul" gavel and sounding block, handcrafted by Worshipful Brother E.
Dale Armstrong, Inspector of the 299th Masonic District in Bakersfield, and
presented on the occasion of a Cornerstone Laying Ceremony at Castlerock
Elementary School on September 17, 1999, and hosted by Exeter Kaweah Lodge
No. 424. Finally, a gavel and wooden burl sounding block with an engraved case,
made from California redwood, and hand-carved by Worshipful Brother David
Isaac, Past Master of Salinas Lodge No. 204, presented to the Grand Master at the
Installation of the Lodge on January 3, 1999.
The Grand Master then continued with the 1999 legislation from the day
before.
The Grand Master called to the East the Most Worshipful Ronald
Robinson, Grand Master of the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California and Hawaii,
Inc. He spoke of the growing amity and friendship between the two Grand Lodges
and the great progress being made in developing solid relationships among the
members of the two Grand Lodges. His remarks were warmly received by those
present. The Grand Master presented to him a Certificate of Recognition as a
Distinguished Guest of the Grand Lodge of California.

Report of the Charters Committee ·
Vandell C. Owen, Chairman of the Committee on Charters, moved that the
approval of the consolidation of Lodges by Grand Master Nahin during his term of
office, be ratified. The motion was duly seconded, and was carried unanimously.
The Grand Master continued with the consideration of the Resolutions
properly before Grand Lodge. When all matters had been considered, the Grand
Master thanked the brethren for their attention during the deliberations. He
announced that the results of the voting would be available after the Installation of
Officers on Wednesday, October 13, 1999. The results would be mailed to the
Lodge Secretaries after the close of the Annual Communication.
At 12:00 Noon the Grand Master called Grand Lodge from labor to
refreshment, to be called on again at I :00 p.m.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

TUESDAY AITERNOON,0CTOBER 12, 1999
At I :00 p.m. the Grand Master called the Grand Lodge from refreshment
to labor, following which the Grand Chaplain offered prayer. The Grand Master
then announced that the Grand Lodge had been raised for the afternoon session by
Worshipful Brother Del Davis, Master of Smyrna Lodge No. 532 and Worshipful
Brother Robert Lam, Master of San Francisco Lodge No. 120. The following
gavels were used: First, a "clown" gavel, presented to the Grand Master on April
9, 1999, at the Grand Master's Reception and Town Hall meeting hosted by Smyrna
Lodge No. 532 at Ceres. The gavel, and its sounding block, were handcrafted by
Brother Wesley Rash, and hand-painted by Shirley Davis, wife of Worshipful
Brother Del Davis, Master of the Lodge. The second gavel was presented to the
Grand Master on May 6, 1999, at a Trout Fry hosted by Burbank Lodge No. 406
in connection with a Grand Master's Reception. It is unique in that it is a carved
white wood gavel, and was hand-carved by Worshipful Brother Harry A. Gunn,
Past Master, and made from lemonwood .. The third gavel was presented on June
18, 1999, at Mariposa, when the Grand Master dedicated the Liberty Hall Masonic
Building in that community as the guest of Mariposa Lodge No. 24. It was crafted
by Worshipful Brother Andy Weare, Past Master, and presented to the Grand
Master along with an old wooden display gavel. Finally, on April 17, 1999, the
Grand Master was presented with a commemorative gavel and sounding block at
the 50th Anniversary Rededication of the Masonic Hall of Van Nuys Lodge No.
450.
The Grand Master called on the Grand Secretary forthe final report of the
Credentials Committee, which showed that there were 362 Lodges registered as
being in attendance, with a total of 1,369 registered Master Masons.

Election of the Grand Master
Deputy Grand Master Alvin J. Weis was nominated for Grand Master by
Most Worshipful E. Arthur Haglund, Past Grand Master. No further nominations
appearing, it was moved, seconded and carried that the nominations be closed, and
that the Grand Secretary be instructed to cast a unanimous ballot for Right
Worshipful Alvin J. Weis to serve as Grand Master for the ensuing Grand Lodge
Year. Upon his acceptance, he was declared to be unanimously elected.

28

Adoption of the 1999-2000 Grand Lodge Budget
The Grand Master called on the Deputy Grand Master, Right Worshipful
Alvin J. Weis, to present the 1999-2000 Grand Lodge Budget. He did so, and a
copy of the budget is found in Appendix B. The Chairman of the Finance
Committee, Worshipful Donald W. Finton, moved the adoption of the 1999-2000
Budget, which was seconded by the Grand Treasurer, and was carried by voice
vote.
Adoption of the 2000-2001 Grand Lodge Per Capita
The Grand Master then called on the Senior Grand Warden, Right
Worshipful David C. Decker to present the 2000-2001 Grand Lodge Per Capita.
He did so, and a copy of the proposal is found in Appendix C.
The Chairman of the Finance Committee, Worshipful Donald W. Finton,
moved the adoption of the 2000-2001 Grand Lodge Per Capita in the amount of
$18.86, which was seconded by the Grand Treasurer, and carried by voice vote.
Election of Officers
The Grand Master then asked the Grand Secretary to explain the balloting
procedure for the election of officers. No ballot would be necessary if the office is
not contested. If more than one nomination is received for an office, ballot cards
will be distributed for the purpose of balloting for that office.

29

Election of Deputy Grand Master
Senior Grand Warden David C. Decker was nominated for Deputy Grand
Master by Most Worshipful Allen B. Gresham, Past Grand Master. No further
nominations appearing, it was moved, seconded and carried that the nominations
be closed, and that the Grand Secretary be instructed to cast a unanimous ballot for
Right Worshipful David C. Decker to serve as Deputy Grand Master for the ensuing
Grand Lodge Year. Upon his .acceptance, he was declared to be unanimously
elected.
Election of Senior Grand Warden
Junior Grand Warden C. Ray Whitaker was nominated for Senior Grand
Warden by Most Worshipful Sam M. Pavlovich, Past Grand Master. No further
nominations appearing, it was moved, seconded and carried that the nominations
be closed, and that the Grand Secretary be instructed to cast a unanimous ballot for
Right Worshipful C. Ray Whitaker to serve as Senior Grand Warden for the
ensuing Grand Lodge Year. Upon his acceptance, he was declared to be
unanimously elected.
Election of Junior Grand Warden
The Grand Master announced that pursuant to Section 510 of the
California Masonic Code, Worshipful Brother Marvin William Holsinger, a Past
Master of Evergreen Lodge No. 259 in Riverside, has been recommended for the
office of Junior Grand Warden of the Grand Lodge of California for the ensuing
Grand Lodge Year. The Grand Master then read the biography previously
circulated in accordance with this section, while Brother Holsinger stood before
Grand Lodge. He was then escorted to the Grand Tiler's Room, while other
nominations were called for. None appearing, it was moved, seconded and carried
that the Grand Secretary be instructed to cast a unanimous ballot for Worshipful
Brother Marvin William Holsinger to serve as Junior Grand Warden forthe ensuing
Grand Lodge Year. Upon his return to the floor of the Grand Lodge, and upon his
acceptance, he was declared unanimously elected by the Grand Master.
Election of Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary, and Grand Lecturer
The Grand Master then announced that pursuant to Section 5 I 0 of the
California Masonic Code, the Executive Committee had recommended that the
following be nominated to serve for the ensuing Grand Lodge Year:

Election of Grand Treasurer
Very Worshipful Herbert P. Wilkins nominated Very Worshipful Thomas
C. Holm to serve as Grand Treasurer for the ensuring Grand Lodge Year. No
further nominations appearing, he moved that the nominations be closed, and that
the Grand Secretary be instructed to cast a unanimous ballot for Thomas C. Holm
to serve as Grand Treasurer. The motion was duly seconded and adopted
unanimously, and upon his acceptance, the Grand Master declared him elected.
Election of Grand Secretary
Most Worshipful Stanley M. Cazneaux, Past Grand Master, nominated
Very Worshipful John L. Cooper III to serve as Grand Secretary for the ensuing
Grand Lodge Year. No further nominations appearing, he moved that the
nominations be closed, and that the Grand Treasurer be instructed to cast a
unanimous ballot for John L. Cooper III to serve as Grand Secretary. The motion
was duly seconded and adopted unanimously, and upon his acceptance, the Grand
Master declared him elected.
Election of Grand Lecturer
Worshipful Edward P. Margherio, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division I,
nominated Very Worshipful Ulysses G. Patropulos to serve as Grand Lecturer for
the ensuing Grand Lodge Year. No further nominations appearing, he moved that
the nominations be closed, and that the Grand Secretary be instructed to cast a
unanimous ballot for Ulysses G. Patropulos to serve as Grand Lecturer. The motion
was duly seconded and adopted unanimously, and upon his acceptance, the Grand
Master declared him elected.
Grand Lodge Called from Labor to Refreshment

the purpose of installing the Grand Lodge Officers for the ensuing Grand Lodge
Year. The Installation was announced as being at 11:00 AM on Wednesday,
October 13, 1999.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Following the newly installed Grand Master's remarks, the Most
Worshipful Melville H. Nahin, Past Grand Master, was presented with his Past
Grand Master's Apron, Jewel, and Wallet Card. Mrs. Alice Nahin was presented
a gift in appreciation of her time and support of her husband and the Grand Lodge
during his year as Grand Master.
Mrs. Virginia Weis, wife of the new Grand Master, was escorted to the
East. She presented him with the gavel which had originally been given to him in
1952 when he was installed Master Councilor of Manteca Chapter, Order of
DeMolay. The gavel was accompanied by a sounding block which had been
presented to the Grand Master when he was installed as Master of AcalanesFellowship Lodge No. 480 in 1981.
The Most Worshipful Mozafar Jandaghi, Grand Master of the Grand
Lodge of Iran (In Exile) in appreciation of the fraternal relations between the two
Grand Lodges, presented a book, A Survey of Persian Handicrafts, to the Grand
Master.
The Installation ceremonies were concluded with the Grand Chaplain
giving the Benediction. The Grand Lodge Officers then retired from the Auditorium
to attend the Gala Reception in the lobby of the California Masonic Memorial
Temple.

Closing of Grand Lodge
At 1:45 pm, Grand Master Alvin J. Weis called Grand Lodge from
refreshment to labor.
Grand Lodge was then closed in ample form.

black hair becomes gray, the athletic body becomes pudgy and soft. But the morals
and the brains, the dedication and the love are still there.
Oh, we've lost an opportunity, I suppose, with the baby-boomers, but
we're getting their children, the "x-generation". Our statistics show, and though
I'm really not one for statistics, our Grand Lodge statistics show that the bulk of our
membership now is coming from the 40 year olds and younger, 42% this year.
Two-thirds of our new members, 67% are under 50. I think that's great, don't you?
We can't stop the aging process, I'm getting older and so are you whether we want
to or not. But we're being replaced and we're going to continue being replaced by
those who are younger, much younger than we. They have found that morality and
integrity is what they want in life. They look, not to their parents, but to their
grandparents in setting the standards. They're coming. And they're coming in
goodly numbers.
The future is clear. The best of times is now. We do live in a wonderful
world.
When I was planning for this year as Grand Master I realized that some
changes had to be made; we all recognize that things that were true 50 years ago
have to be modified to bring them "up to snuff." And we have attempted to do that
this year.
In addition to our continuing support for those diamonds in our crown, our
Masonic Homes and our Foundation, we have initiated new programs and given
impetus to others. Our Childhood Identification Program which started with two
units this year has been increased to six through the generosity of Metropolitan and
Washington Lodges and of Riviera Lodge which donated two units and they are all
in full use on a weekly basis. We have been able to increase the Masonic Student
Assistance Training Programs, with great cooperation from our Masonic Homes
Board of Trustees and our Foundation Board of Trustees from eight to twelve
sessions each year, a 50% increase, plus two booster sessions. We have continued
our support for the scholarships that have afforded us the opportunity to contribute
greatly to our community and, along with our support for the Teacher of the Year
Programs, have enabled us get out into the schools and to meet the people, most of
whom had little know ledge about Freemasonry, and to show the great flag, not only
of this country, but ofFreemasonry. And there's an awful lot that we have had the
opportunity to show and to share.
This year we've started three new programs, I kind of call them my Grand
Lodge tripod, programs which I think are absolutely necessary for the success of
this fraternity in California. The first is an "outreach" erogram. We call it the
Professional Public Relations Program of the Family of Freemasonry, a
combination of twelve Masonic entities forming together to get the word out, to
show our neighbors and our friends, our co-workers and our co-parishioners, who
it is we are and what we do, and we do a great deal, and they're getting to know it.
We're doing our newspaper ads, our outdoor advertising, our interviews on talk
shows - just a couple of months ago we were on talk radio on KGO here in San
Francisco but with a frequency that covered the whole west coast of the United
States discussing what Freemasonry is all about with call-in questions- surprisingly
so all positive questions, ads in the Southwest Airline magazine and beautiful
colored ads in the news magazines- - Time, Newsweek and U.S. News and World
Report. We're telling what our great organization of Freemasonry is, what it does

and what it strives to be. We are getting our message out! We are taking our "light
from under the bushel!" And we will continue to do so because Alvin and David
and Ray want to do so and know the importance of continuing this program as do
all the organizations which have supported us to the tune of some $850,000.00 over
a three year period. And that includes the $1.00 per capita that I asked you some
two years ago to give us for this program and to which you enthusiastically agreed.
overwhelmingly ,and have supported strongly since its inception. You know no one
will join an organizatio!1 he doesn't .know ~xists, and no one wil! join an
organization when what httle he knows 1s negative. That would be stup1dand the
people of California are not stupid. They will come. They are coming. Have no
doubt about that. The first leg of our tripod stands strong.
Then we realized that if we did have an influx of members, what would we
do with them? Would we Jet them sit on the sidelines once they became Master
Masons in name at least and have nobody approach them, nobody involve them in
Freemasonry? We surely would Jose them quickly if we did that, wouldn'twe? So
the next step we had to undertake was how to handle the Masons, the new men, the
men who took their degrees, the men who wanted to become a part of our great
fraternity, what to do with them once they became mem.bers. And from tha! came
the idea of our Town Halls, 14 of them we've had this year from San Diego to
Ukiah from Chico to Anaheim. We've kind of covered the waterfront
geo~phically this year with our Town Halls, none taking place more than 50 miles
from any given lodge hall. During those Saturday morning sessionswe've talked
with many of our brethren from Entered Apprentices to Past Grand Lodge Officers,
intensive sessions where you've discussed with us and we wi~ you, what.we. c~uld
do to improve the workings of the Grand Lodge, the work~gs of the md1:v1dual
lodges. This was not a replacement for the wonderful Warden s Retreats which we
have, nor replacement for the very much needed and utilized Officers Mana&ement
Workshops. This'was a friend-to-friend program from an internal standpomt and
we made not only a Jot of friends but we learned of many questions you wanted
answered, the many problems you wanted solved, and in tum we endeavored to
give you the necessary information. One of the brothers of this Grand Lodge, a
"retread" who will again be Master of his lodge, saw fit to attend ten of the 14
Town Halls and when I asked him why he was attending so many of them, he
advised me that he had learned more from the Town Halls than he learned going up
the line in his lodge, attending the Officers Manag~ment. Workshops .an.d the
Retreats, more information, more answers, more gettmg thmgs done w1thm the
lodge to effect a successful lodge program. We discovered your problems and we
tried to help you and we will hopefully continue to help you so that your lodges and
its programs will flourish. The second leg of the tripod stands firm and strong.
So we kind of took care of the external and the internal portions of our
needs in Freemasonry in California. But that's this year. What's going t~ happen
in the future? Who's going to take charge? What programs are g<?mg to be
effective? We learned very quickly that we needed a Long Range Plannmg tyre of
organization to form our third leg of th~ tripod and we develo~ w~at I st1l call
the Five-Year Plan led by some outstandmg members of our organ1zat1on., and I aJ!l
indeed grateful to them for the hard work they have put m. You have re~e1ved the.rr

with you, but this year we just don't have that luxury of time. They've done an

One hundred twenty of us, members of our Grand Lodge family traveled
to the Hot~ Land a~hieving a religi<;>us Masonic experience that it is im~ssible to

of all denominations, of all persuasions. We saw a lot and did a lot in fourteen

and came back as one, one small section of that united family of Freemasonry.
This year has been a busy one. We have had eight 75-year Diamond
Jubilee presentations,_ a large number of 50-year Golden Veteran Awards, 18
cornerstone ceremomes, 28 Masonic Lodge and four Scottish Rite Valley
installations, lots and lots of activities, some 287 by our Grand Secretary's count.
Tho.se are numbers and h~ve been great experiences for us of the Grand Lodge
Family, but those are for this year. Where do we go from here? One thing for sure.
Let's ~et two phrases out of our vocabularies once and for all, I) "We have never
done it that way" and 2) "We've always done it that way."
w_e must adopt a positive attitude. We must be deliberate and thorough
.
10 our studies. We must become careful and decide upon recommended changes
!l8 clo~ to unanimously as possible as we do our legislative program this year and
it's a big one. We must have a commitment to achieve our goals and implement the
changes agreed to.
We must change our attitudes from apathy to action. We need, we really
need a "~ho~lder to the wheel" eff<~rt ~stead of the often typical "shrug of the
shoulder' att~tud~. We must stop wnngmg our hands about membership declines,
lodge consohdations, poor turnouts at our meetings. It's time to stop complaining
~.d start doing_ something about it. California Freemasonry stands for greatness;
it is a comm~1ty asset con_iposed of responsibl~ law abiding citizens which by its
presence provides a me~~~ful force for. pubhc good. C~lifornia Freemasonry
stands for mo!'ll respons1b1hty, for charity, for fellowship and friendship, for
honesty and fairness, for courtesy and concern. California Freemasonry stands for
excellence,_ for ~igher quality, to be the best possible striving to make good men
better. Cahforn1a Freemasonry stands for better understanding among men to aid
mankind's ~earch in God's universe for identity, for development and for destiny.
What then is our future? Can we control the wheel of destiny? What must we do
to surviv~? . Vtf e must be a .quality organization of substance and dignity which
oife.rs to ~ndlVlduals and society the physical and moral means for intellectual and
spmtual improvement.
We must champion and foster the cause of individual liberty and justice
for the betterment of mankind by encouraging men ofcharacter with a sense of duty
to contribute their resources, service and know ledge for the benefit of all society,
We must provide Masons with the opportunity to become better men, to share

fellowship and friendship with like minded men throughout the world - and there
are presently 4 million of us; to stimulate their individual interests and personal
growth and enlightenment, their personal satisfaction along with the sense of
djrection through life. We must teach a basic philosophy of life that promotes
responsibility, honesty and fairness in all of our dealings along with courtesy and
concern for others. To fulfill this mission we must unite and mobilize. All of the
Family of Freemasonry must make a greater commitmentto Freemasonry. Perhaps
the greatest difficulty in effecting the change that we need lies in our thinking
which has been molded over the past years. We can and must make changes
through planned actions. Masonic leaders must base their actions on the
recognition that the individual Mason is more important than ever to the lodge. Let
us always remember and make this permanent m our memories - a Mason is not
dependent upon us, we are dependent upon him. A Mason brings us his wants. It
is our responsibility to satisfy his needs. The greatest disservice to ourselves and
to our fraternity would be to concede that any problem is insurmountable and that
there are no solutions to be found.
No, our problems won't be solved overnight, no special committee is
going to make them go away. Our public relations policy is going to take a while
to take effect. People are going to have to get to know their neighbors, their coreligionists, the men they bowl with, the women they shop with, who wear the
Masonic insignia. They're going to have to get to know who and what we are and
what we represent. Problem solving, sound planning, hard work, determination
and even making some hard choices will allow us to achieve a true Masonic
renewal, to once again be known as the quality organization we once were and to
build the kind of effective organization that we can all be proud of, an organization
that will appeal to the good men of all ages as it has been in all ages past.
Always remember, and I stress this so very often, that we are a Family of
Freemasonry, not just a group of different organizations and whatever your favorite
Masonic organization may be, we must all work together toward its revitalization
for in "recreating the wheel" of Freemasonry we shall certainly recreate all of its
spokes. As Freemasonry lives, grows and prospers, so do we, all of the Masonic
organizations in the Family of Freemasonry live, grow and prosper.
And when do we begin? Today! Right now, this very minute! Have you
ever noticed that we call today the present. God's gift to us is the 24 hours we live
each day. His present to us.
This has been a year of challenge, but it has been rewarding and for that
I am grateful, not only to those who have invited us to participate in the many
events we have scheduled and performed, but also in the support of the many, like
you today, who have been at those activities and participated in them and proudly
have shown the flag of the Grand Lodge ofCalifornia. Each Grand Master believes
that he has a good Masonic Family, an outstanding Masonic Family. But I don't
believe it - I know it! From the Assistant Grand Organist and the Assistant Grand
Tiler to the Deputy Grand Master, each has been supportive, each has been there
when I needed him and each has held me up as did the supporters of Moses of old,
to make sure that the battle was well fought, that battle was won. And I am indeed
grateful to each of these men and most especially to their ladies without whom this
year could not have had the success and accomplishments that it has had. I truly
love them - each and every one of them.

TRIBUT E TO THE FLAG OF OUR COUNTR Y

Melville H. Nahin, Grand Master
My Country 'Tis of Thee
Sweet Land of Liberty
Of Thee I Sing
A. ~ation conceived in liberty, born out of faith in God, and dedicated to
the proposition that all men are created equal and thus entitled to freedom.
It is with this freedom in mind that we pause at the very beginning of this
Gr:and Communication to pay tribute to the flag which represents every freedom of
this country.
. A freedom that has brought to its people a degree of prosperity and
happmess never even approached under any other banner.
A country which derives its just powers from the consent of the governed.
A country with a constitution that is the greatest single document in the
entire struggle of mankind for orderly self-government.
A country where people are risking their very lives to come here and live
in freedom.
While it is valid for a country to have quotas on the number of people who
enter that country- there probably is no greater compliment to us or to any other
country than the fact that men and women from all over the world risk their very
life and limb to come to America.
This inward migration has been effectively set to music in the theme song
of a popular movie of a few years ago, Neil Diamond's The Jazz Singer.
Its lyrics include:
Everywhere around the world
They're coming to America
Every time that flag's unfurled
They're coming to America
Got a dream to take them there
They're coming to America
Got a dream they've come to share
They're coming to America
They're coming to America.
Where else, my Brothers, are people risking their very lives to get into a
country?
Wh~n ~e think of~is flag and a!I it. represents, _no greater example can be
.
given for b~hef m and sacnfice of the pnnc1ples on which the country is founded
these
th~ ~e ultimate sacrifice that has been paid in lives to uphold and defend
pnnc1ples of freedom. Examples of these sacrifices for freedom are legend in the
history of this country.
~amples would include 1918 - World War I. With Germany driving
toward ~~s, between 6000 ~d 8000 Americans gave their lives at Belleau Wood
and therr !me held. The Amencans counter-attacked at Chateau Thierry, Paris was

saved and thereafter the Germans were on the defensive.
The answer to freedom's call was heard again in 1945 - World War II.
More than 5000 men of the Third, Fourth, and Fifth U.S. Marine Divisions gave
their lives to capture an eight-square mile island called Iwo Jima to halt the
J~ese tighter plans that were taking off from the island, and we then used the
airstrips to protect our bombers.
America defended again in 1950 in Korea. With the Allies pushed against
U.S. 10th Corps made a lightning surprise amphibious landing at Inchon.

Incredible because the landings had to ~e timed to the ~inute beca~se of the widely

The spirit of our armed forces was called on again in 1968 - Republic of
South Vietnam. For 77 days U.S. Marines defended their base at Khe Sanh, one of
the longest battles of the war and held on until the communists withdrew.
Again, April 24, 1980 in the Dasht-e-Kavir desert of Iran near the

in an attempt to rescue 53 fellow Americans being held hostage in Tehran.
Since then our young men have fought in the Persian Gulf in 1991, and

and humanity.

PROCLAMATION

California Masonic Foundation Month
U.S. CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH

HOW MUCH IS A CHILD WORTH?
"To relieve distress is a duty incumbent upon all men, but particularly on all Masons.·
How much is a child worth. or perhaps a few children. or perhaps a whole group or children? Can it be measured in terms of
dollars and cents or must it always be in tenms of"blood, sweat and tears?"
In recent months, the newspapers and television have emboldened us with screeching headfiMS and news b<iefs about
children in public schools throughout our country arming themselves with weapons and shooting those weapons without any particular
reason and into their classmates. into their friends and church goers. We don't know why. I suppose each child has a background
that must be considered, but we are in this state requiring each of us to acknowledge the problem of what is happening to our young
people, or at least some of them, and then doing something about il
We have had deaths in Springfield, Oregon and in Jonesboro, Arkansas • indiscriminate killing. We wonder whether those
kids could have been prevented from doing as they have done in the destruction of the lives of others and yes, their own destruction.
We wonder if their schools had our Masonic Student Assistance Training Programs whether those children, those •at risk children·,
could have been identified before the acts of violence and thereby directed into help, into much needed help.
We of California Masonry are indeed fortunate that we have at our fingertips, a member of the Family of Freemasonry, which
is doing something about this problem. We are fortunate that we have the California Masonic Foundation. Initially ft was conceived
to award scholarships to needy high school students before they entered college and thereby make the road to education, to ie.nong
easier and the road to successful adulthood, a safer road to travel.
In recent years we have spread into the Masonic Student Assistance Training Program bringing together educators and
administrators from all over the state to our Home in Covina. to leach them, to help them teach each other, to determine those "at risk
children• and thereby save many lives of those who might be the perpetrators and of course, as a result. the lives and health of the
otherwise victims. Our Masonic Student Assistance Training Program ia indeed one recognized throughout the Masonic wor1d and
throughout the educational wor1d, as a great assistance, as a great provider for assistance to others, in helping our children grow into
helpful and productive lives. We have so many testimonies, too many to count and hopefully many more to come.
We are proud of this program and proud even more to know that because of your assistance, you of the Masonic Family, we
are now able ID enlarge the program by fifty percent, to have twelve sessions in 1999 instead of the pl'8Yious eight as well as booster

Our nation has now been in existence for almost 21/4 centuries. It has withstood the test of battle; it has withstood
the test of time.
As we look about us in the world today, we must be thankful for the steadiness of our great nation. Whatever
troubles and dissension we have. and we certainly do have them, whatever tragedies and political upheavals we
have, and we have those too, the government of our great United States proceeds in an orderly fashion. Based
on a Constitution that all citizens recognize and accept as a guarantee of their freedom and the framework of their
liberty, the form of our government remains a dependable and known constant. It is an intimately familiar starting
point from which each of us may travel forth to experiment with and entertain new ideas, knowing we can always
return to the safety of the tested structure of our great Constitution.
This most successful form of self-government so far designed by man is still being pulled and tugged at by citizens
who wish to change or modify this structure in some way, who believe they can bring the nation closer to the
realization of its ideals by adding to or amending the constitutional framework on which our government exists.
We are constantly exposed to the arguments and pressures of many groups wanting to make such changes.
Some we will consider. Others we will reject. But as Americans, as individuals, we have the right, the freedom,
the liberty to listen and to lend our strength to a cause, without fear. Our Constitution provides us with all the
latitude we need; for this reason it has long endured and pray God it will long endure.
In recognition of the rare and precious benefits we derive from that noble document, I proclaim the month of
September , 1999 to be
U.S. CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH

sessions.

Our California Masonic Foundation Is a jewel in our crown and we are proud ID acknowledge itto all of the Lodges of this state.
1rs your Foundation.
I therefore take wfth great pride the privilege in PROCLAIMING the month of AUGUST 1999 as
CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION MONTH
and urge each of you to think of what you can do to help save our children. \II/hat is a child worth? Only by your actions in the support
of the California Masonic Foundation will we know the answer to that question. As I ponder the question. I ask myself, "what are my
children, my grandchildren worth?"

and direct all constituent lodges in California to participate individually, by Districts or by combined Districts, in
appropriate observances and meaningful patriotic programs to which the public shall be invited.
I further direct that this Proclamation shall be read at the August and September, 1999 Stated Meetings and
wherever possible be reprinted in lodge bulletins for September.
Patriotism and love of freedom and individual liberty are not and never will be dead in America; they are alive and
well and always shall be in the hearts and in the actions of Freemasons.
Dated this 1•day of July, 1999.

I urge you to support the activities of the California Masonic Foundabon, this month and every month throughout the Masonic
year. In Testimony whereof I have heretofore set my hand and caused the seal of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and
Accepted Masons or California to be affixed this first day or May. 1999.
Sincerely and Fraternally\\ .

REPORT OF THE DEPUTY GRAND MASTER
1999-2000 Grand Lodge Budget
Alvin J. Weis, Deputy Grand Master

Brethren, Section 7040 of the California Masonic Code requires the
Deputy Grand Master to prepare the Grand Lodge Budget for submission to Grand
Lodge each year. A copy of that Budget was sent to you more than 30 days ago in
advance of the convening of Grand Lodge, as required by our law.
On August20 each Lodge was mailed the proposed Grand Lodge Budget
for 1999/2000. The funding for that budget came primarily from the July I, 1999,
per capita which has already been paid by our lodges. The budget as presented
therefore reflects an accurate statement of income, and the projected expenditures
are also an accurate reflection of our anticipated costs. As you will note, despite
several thousand fewer members this year, the budget holds the line on
expenditures, and actually represents a reduction over the previous year.
The budget represents an investment in people and programs by our Grand
Lodge. It is prudent and responsible, but at the same time, it reflects our
commitment to the future of Freemasonry in this jurisdiction. It represents no
compromise on quality, but insures that our future leaders have the resources to
carry through on today's promises.
I pledge to you my continued watchful care over the resources of this
Grand Lodge, and I ask you to support the budget which is before you.

In accordance with the principles above, the 1999-2000 Proposed Budget recommends that the per
capita for 2000 be established at $18.86, which is a 4% increase. With income expected to drop by

SUBJECT:

Section 7040 of the California Masonic Code requires the Deputy Grand Master to prepare the
Grand Lodge Budget for submission to Grand Lodge at the next Annual Communication. That
budget is prepared with the assistance of the Grand Lodge Committee on Finance and the Grand
Treasurer. It is passed on the per capita adopted by Grand Lodge at the previous Annual
Communication, and collected from each Lodge in accordance with the number of Master Masons
carried on the rolls of the Lodge as of June 30 next preceding the forthcoming Annual
Communication. At the 149 111 Annual Communication in October, 1998, the per capita was
established at $18.14 (including $1.30 for the California Freemason magazine). As of June 30,
1999, our Lodge reported 95,244 Master Masons, less 2,614 whose dues had been remitted. The net
assessable membership is therefore 92,630 Master Masons (a 4.3% decline from a year ago).
1999-2000 Grand Lodge Budget:
The 1999 per capita of$ I 8. l 4 assessed on the basis of92,630 Master Masons is expected to produce
a revenue ofSl,680,308. This year's per capita revenue is $14,843 less than last year due to the
decline in assessable members. Miscellaneous income, including interest income and the dividend
from Nob Hill Masonic Management, Inc., will result in a total estimated income ofSl,864,338.
The estimated expenses for 1999-2000 are $1,575,692, plus $125,051 for publishing the California
Freemason magazine. The difference between income and total expenses is $163,595, and is
allocated to Depreciation Reserve ($80,000), and the Grand Lodge Endowment Fund ($83,595). The
Grand Lodge Endowment Fund was established to help offset future declines in membership, thus
helping to soften the impact of the rapid decline in membership expected to continue over the next
few years. The Endowment Fund was established by a vote of Grand Lodge to smooth out future
increases in per capita by reserving some present income for future need.

Alvin J. Weis
Dep ty Grand Master

support programs important to your Lodge and to our Grand Lodge.
As you study the attached pages, please be reminded that figures represent many hours of hard work
to bring you a responsible budget based on the best information possible. It represents a
commitment to prudently manage the resources of Grand Lodge now, and for the future. And it
represents my commitment to you to continue to strengthen our beloved Fraternity by ensuring a
sound financial base of operations for your Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

The Grand Treasurer is charged with the responsibility of reporting on the
financial condition of Grand Lodge and its related investments, businesses and
charities at the Annual Communication. This includes the financial statements,
operations and planning for Grand Lodge, as well as for those of the Masonic
Homes of California, the Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund, the California
Masonic Retirement Plan, the California Masonic Foundation, the California
Masonic Memorial Temple, and the Nob Hill Masonic Management, Inc. (please
refer to the opinion letters attached in the annual Proceedings by your auditors).
The reports and comments of the Grand Treasurer are based on the official
examinations and statements of our Certified Puhl ic Accountants whose reports are
an integral part of the Grand Treasurer's Report. Their audits cover the years most
recently ended and contain both a complete statement of assets under management
as well as a record of the income and expenses for the period.
As delegates to the Annual Communication, you are, in effect, the
shareholders of Grand Lodge and its entities. You are encouraged, and it is
recommended therefore, that you read and review this report. Your observations
are appreciated.
Both the Grand Lodge and each ofits related entities are in sound financial
condition. The extent and size of our investments, businesses, and most
importantly our charitable activities were financially possible in large measure due
to the generosity of prior generations. To ensure the future of these fine programs,
we must continue our Masonic tradition of financial support.
Respectfully submitted,
Thomas C. Holm, Grand Treasurer

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California:
We have audited the accompanying consolidating statement of financial position of The Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the Grand Lodge)
(a nonprofit, unincorporated fraternal organization) and Subsidiary as of October 31, 1999, and the
related consolidating statement of activities and changes in net assets and consolidated statement
of cash flows for the year then ended. These financial statements and the schedules referred to
below are the responsibility of the Grand Lodge's management. Our responsibility is to express an
opinion on these financial statements and schedules based on our audit.
We conducted our audit in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those
standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes examining,
on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An
audit also includes assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by
management, as well as evaluating the overall financial statement presentation. We believe that
our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.

In our opinion. the financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material respects, the
individual and consolidated financial positions of the Grand Lodge and Subsidiary as of
October 31, 1999, and the individual and consolidated results of their operations and their
consolidated cash flows for the year then ended in conformity with generally accepted accounting
principles.
Our audit was made for the purpose of forming an opinion on the basic financial statements taken
as a whole. The accompanying Supplemental Schedules I to V are presented for purposes of
additional analysis and are not a required part of the basic financial statements. This information
has been subjected to the auditing procedures applied in our audit of the basic financial statements
and, in our opinion, is fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the basic financial
statements taken as a whole.

1. ORGANIZATION AND SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:
Organization
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the
Gran~ Lodge) is a n~nprofit ~corporated fraternal organization and is governed by a
constitution ai:d ordinances setttng forth its jurisdiction and authority. The jurisdiction of the
Gran~ Lod~e rncludes all l?~ges and Ma~ons within the state of California, and members of lodges
of ~o.rrua, wher~ver _residing. Nob Hill Masonic Management, Inc. (Nob Hill), a for-profit
~omia corpor~tton, IS ~e wholly owned subsidiary of the Grand Lodge. Nob Hill operates the
~orrua Masoruc M~monal Temple (the Temple) auditorium. parking garage, exhibit hall and
various rental properties under the terms of an operating lease with the Temple.
The Grand Lo~ge ~rovides general and administrative services to its related entities: the Masonic
Homes ~f California .(Masonic Homes); the Temple; the California Masonic Foundation (the
Foundation); the California Masonic Retirement Plan; Nob Hill; and the Masonic Homes Pooled
lnc?me Fund (collectively, the Masonic Entities). These services are reimbursed by the related
enttty.
Principles of Consolidation
The ~al statements include the accounts of the Gr~d Lodge and its wholly owned
subs1~. ~material intercompany amounts have been eliminated. The accounts of the other
Masoruc Enttttes have not been included in the Grand Lodge's financial statements because the
Grand Lodge does not have both control and an economic interest in such related entities.
Income Tax Status
The G~and Lodge has been granted tax-exempt status for both federal income and California
franchis~ tax purposes. Nob Hill income taxes are accounted for under Statement of Financial
Accounting Standards (SFAS) No. 109, "Accounting for Income Taxes."

Property and equipment, including leasehold improvements, are recorded at cost and are
depreciated using the straight-line method over estimated useful lives of three to twenty-five years.
Collections
The Grand Lodge owns a collection of jewelry and other objects, most of which have historical
significance. The jewelry collection is used in Lodge ceremonies, and the other objects are .
displayed in the Temple Museum. Purchases of collection items are reflected as decreases I.I\
unrestricted net assets in the year in which the items are acquired. The Grand Lodge does not
recognize these assets as contributions as they are protected and preserved, held for public
exhibition, and are subject to an organizational policy that requires proceeds from the sale of
collection items to be used to acquire other collection items. Accessions and deaccessions during
1999 were not significant.
Deferred Per Capita Revenue
Dues received for the subsequent fiscal year are recorded as deferred per capita revenue until
earned.
Unrestricted Net Assets
Unrestricted net assets are available to support all activities of the Grand Lodge, including amounts
designated by the Grand Lodge as follows:

• The Gnind Lodge Endowment Fund (the Endowment Fund) was established at the Grand
Lodge's October 1993 Annual Communication. If in any fiscal year there is an excess of
support and revenues over expenses, as defined, the excess shall be added to the Endowment
Fund if the cumulative excess exceeds $700,000. For the year ended October 31, 1999, the
excess added to the Endowment Fund was $261,438 resulting in an ending balance of
$1,747,704.

• The 150 Yearbook Fund, which had a balance of $137,747 as of October31, 1999. This fund is
expected to be used in 2000 to defray the costs of commemorative items.

Inventory
Inventory is stated at cost on a first-in, first-out basis.
Investments
Investments in marketable securities are stated at fair value based on quoted market prices. Gains
or lo~ses th~t result from mar~et fluctuations are recognized in the period such fluctuations occur.
Realize~ gains. or losses resulting from sales or maturities of securities are calculated on an adjusted
cost bas1S. Ad1usted cost IS the market value of the security at the beginning of the year, or the cost

Temporarily restricted net assets represent co~tri~tions whose use by the Grand Lodg~ is limited
by donor-imposed stipulations that either expire with the passage of ttme or can be fulfilled and
removed by the Grand Lodge pursuant to those stipulations.

The Grand Lodge reports gifts of cash and other assets as restricted support ii such gifts are
received with donor stipulations that limit the use of the donated assets. When a donor restriction
expires, that is, when a stipulated time restriction ends or a purpose restriction is accomplished,
temporarily restricted net assets are reclassified to unrestricted net assets and reported as net assets
released from restriction. Temporarily restricted contributions are reported as temporarily
restricted support and net assets released from restrictions during the period when the restriction is
met in the same period as the contribution is received.

On June 30, 1998, Nob Hill (the lessee) and the Temple (the lessor) entered into an operating lease,
expiring June 30, 2003, of the Temple auditorium, exhibit hall, parking garage and various rental
properties. Under the terms of the lease, Nob Hill is required to pay rent equal to 90 percent of the
gross rental revenues in excess of a base amount of $860,000 per year, adjusted annually for
inflation, until Nob Hill has paid $240,000, after which the payment shall be one-third of the
remaining gross rental revenues. Beginning in 1998, the aggregate rent calculated under this
formula is subject to a limit that increases with inflation. For the year ended October 31, 1999, lease
expense totaled $430,000.

6. INCOMETAXES:

The provision for 1999 income taxes for Nob Hill, which is based on statutory rates, is $124,342.
The tax effect of temporary differences between the financial statements and tax returns is
insignificant.
7. PENSION PLAN:
The Grand lodge, Masonic Homes, the Foundation, the Temple and Nob Hill sponsor a defined
benefit pension plan (the Plan) that covers all employees. Benefits are to be paid to eligible
employees at retirement based primarily upon years of service and compensation levels near
retirement. Contributions to the Plan reflect benefits attributed to employees' services to date, as
well as services expected to be provided in the future. Plan assets consist primarily of equity and
fixed income mutual funds.
Pension expense and other activity of the Plan for the year ended October 31, 1999, included the
following components:
Pension expense
Employer contribution
Plan participants' contributions

We have audited the accompanying statements of financial position of Masonic Homes of
California (a California nonprofit corporation) as of June 30, 1999 and 1998, and the related
statements of activities and changes in net assets and of cash flows for the years then ended. These
financial statements are the responsibility of Masonic Homes of California management. Our
responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audits.
We conducted our audits in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those
standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes examining,
on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An
audit also includes assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by
management, as well as evaluating the overall financial statement presentation. We believe that
our audits provide a reasonable basis for our opinion.

The assets, liabilities and net assets of Masonic Homes are presented in the accompanying
statement of financial position as follows:
•

Generrd and Earthquake Funds-Resources are available to support the operations of the
homes at Union City and Covina, California. The net assets of the general fund are
primarily unrestricted.
Permanent Endowment Fund-Ordinances of the Grand Lodge provide that no portion of
the principal of the Permanent Endowment Fund shall be expended for any purpose, and
income from the principal shall be used only for the maintenance and general operation of
Masonic Homes. Therefore, the historical dollar value of contributions made to the
Permanent Endowment Fund are permanently restricted, while the accumulated
investment earnings and net market appreciation are temporarily restricted until the
associated donor restriction on use has been satisfied.

in the period in which such fluctuations occur. Realized gains or losses resulting from sales or
maturities of securities are calculated on an adjusted-cost basis. Adjusted cost is the market value
of the security at the beginning of the year or the cost if purchased during the year.
Assets Held for Sale
Assets held for sale consist primarily of tangible property received from residents, including real
estate, that is held for sale. Assets are recorded at appraised value on date of assignment.
Property and Equipment
Property and equipment are carried at cost and are depreciated on the straight-line method over
the following estimated lives:
Buildings and improvements
Equipment
Furniture and fixtures
Vehicles

Union City Fund-The Union City Fund provides for the operation, rehabilitation,
preservation and betterment of the home at Union City, as deemed necessary. The Union
City Fund was established with bequests from the estates of Hugo M. Lorber and
Florence V. Grider, which provided that the a.mounts be used for the home for adults at
Union City, California. Because the purpose restrictions related to the principal of the
bequests have been met and no donor restrictions were placed on the investment earnings
and net market appreciation from the principal, the net assets of the Union City Fund are
unrestricted. The net assets of this fund have been designated by the Board for construction
purposes.

•

Rntricted Trust Funds-Restricted Trust Funds include bequests made for various
restricted purposes and various irrevocable trusts of which Masonic Homes is the trustee.
Th~ historic d~llar value of bequests is permanently restricted for investment in perpetuity,

while the earnings from the bequests are either restricted for scholarship purposes or
available for unrestricted use. Masonic Homes' interest in the irrevocable trusts is
temporarily restricted as to time. Once received, the contribution is temporarily restricted
or unrestricted according to the donor stipulations.
Cash and Equivalents
Cash equivalents consist of highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or
less. Cash and equivalents, for purposes of the statement of cash flows, include unrestricted and
restricted cash.
Restricted cash includes residents' accounts at Union City and Covina, which comprise
unexpended portions of monthly allowances made to residents and a construction retainer account
related to the construction at the home for adults at Union City, California. For the residents'
accounts, a corresponding liability for such agency funds is included in accounts payable and
accrued liabilities.
Investments
Investments in debt and equity securities are stated at estimated fair market value based on quoted
market prices. Investments received through gifts are recorded at estimated fair market value at
the date of donation. Unrealized gains or losses that result from market fluctuations are recorded

107

5-50years

3-25
5-20

2- 7

Other Assets
Other assets consist primarily of notes receivable, resident-assigned assets awaiting liquidation, life
insurance policies on residents, and fine art at the two homes.
Other assigned assets are recorded at fair market value on the date of assignment Fine art is
recorded at appraised value at the date of donation.
Deferred Revenue from Pooled Income Fund
Deferred revenue from pooled income fund represents the discount for future investment earnings
on Masonic Homes' remainder interest in the Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund (the Pooled
Income Fund) (see Note 4). Masonic Homes has determined the a.mount deferred using investment
returns consistent with the composition of asset portfolios, single or joint life expectancy from IRS
Publication 1457 tables, and discount rates of 7.7 and 7.0 percent at June 30, 1999 and 1998,
respectively.
Liability to Beneficiary of Split-Interest Agreements
Liability to beneficiaries of split-interest agreements represents the income beneficiaries' interest in
various charitable remainder trusts of which Masonic Homes is the trustee (see Note 4). The
liability is calculated as the present value of the estimated future cash flows to be distributed to the
income beneficiaries over their expected lives. Masonic Homes has determined the a.mount of the
liability using investment returns consistent with the composition of the asset portfolios, single or
joint life expectancies from IRS Publication 1457, Table S, or IRS Publication 1458, Table D, as
applicable, and discount rates of 6.4 and 7.0 percent at June 30, 1999 and 1998, respectively.
Deferred Revenue from Assigned Assets
The fair market value of real and personal property assigned to Masonic Homes by residents
entering into a continuing care contract is deferred and amortized over the actuarially determined
individual or joint and last survivor life expectancy (using the straight-line method based on the

108

-5-

-4State of California Department of Social Services life expectancy table), with anv unamortized
balance recognized as income upon death of the individual or last survivor. ·
Temporarily Restricted Net Assets
Temporarily restricted net assets represent contributions whose use by Masonic Homes is limited
by donor-imposed stipulations that either expire with the passage of time or can be fulfilled and
removed by actions of Masonic Homes pursuant to those stipulations (see Note 5).
Permanently Restricted Net Assets
Permanently restricted net assets are restricted by the donor for investment in perpetuity (see
Note6).

Use of Estimates
The preparation of financial statements in conformity with genei:ally accepted accounting
principles requires management to make estimates and assumptions. These estimates :u'd
assumptions affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and discl~ure of contingent assets
and liabilities at the date of the financial statements. Actual results could differ from those
estimates.

1. ORGANIZATION:

3. INVESTMENTS IN MARKET ABLE SECURITIES:

The Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund (the Fund) was organized in 1974 as a trust. Donors
contribute irrevocable remainder interests in property while retaining an income interest for life for
one or more beneficiaries. The donors are entitled to a tax deduction equivalent to the present
value of the remainder interest in the property contributed to the Fund.

following:

The property transferred by a donor is held in trust by the Board of Trustees of the Fund and is
commingled with and invested and reinvested with other properties transferred to the Fund. All
dividend and interest income of the Fund is distributed quarterly to the income beneficiaries, based
on their proportionate share of the Fund. Upon the death of each donor's last income beneficiary,
the remainder interest is distributed to Masonic Homes of California, a charitable corporation.
2. SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:

Investments at December 31, 1998, are presented at estimated fair value and are composed of the
Fixed income mutual funds
Equity mutual funds

$5,649,569

Total

4. RELATED PARTY:
In 1998, administrative costs for the Fund totaled $107,499. Of this amount, $35,327 was paid by
Masonic Homes of California and $72,172 was paid by the Fund.

Basis of Presentation
The Fund acts in the capacity of an agent on behalf of the life and remainder beneficiaries of the
Fund. The accompanying financial statements include the activities and trust principal for the
period presented.
Investments
Investments in marketable securities are stated at estimated fair market value based on quoted
market prices. Property received through gifts is recorded at estimated fair value at the date of
donation. Gains or losses resulting from sales or market fluctuations are recognized in the period
such sales or market fluctuations occur.
Income Taxes
The Fund is administered in conformity with all provisions of the Internal Revenue Code, Internal
Revenue Regulations and Rulings, procedures and guidelines covering pooled income funds. The
Fund pays no income tax on income distributed to the income beneficiaries or on long-term capital
gains. Applicable federal and state income taxes are paid by the beneficiaries on their share of
distributed income.

California Masonic Foundation:
We have audited the accompanying statement of financial position of California Masonic
Foundation (a California not-for-profit corporation) as of June 30, 1999, and the related statements
of activities and changes in net assets and cash flows for the year then ended. These financial
statements are the responsibility of the organization's management. Our responsibility is to
express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audit
We conducted our audit in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those
standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes examining,
on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An
audit also includes assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by
management, as well as evaluating the overall financial statement presentation. We believe that
our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.
In our opinion, the financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material respects, the
financial position of California Masonic Foundation as of June 30, 1999, and the changes in its net
assets and its cash flows for the year then ended in conformity with generally accepted accounting
principles.

Our audit was made for the purpose of forming an opinion on the basic financial statements taken
as a whole. Supplementary fund information included in the accompanying statement of financial
position, statement of activities and changes in net assets, and Schedules I and II is presented for
purposes of additional analysis and is not a required part of the basic financial statements. This
information has been subjected to the auditing procedures applied in our audit of the basic
financial statements and, in our opinion, is fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the
basic financial statements taken as a whole.

CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATIO N
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENT S
