1. ORGANIZA TION AND SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICAN T ACCOUNTIN G POLICIES:
Organization
The California Masonic Foundation (the Foundation) was established in 1968 by the Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the Grand Lodge). The Foundation is
formed as a nonprofit charitable corporation to further all phases of education, charity and science.
Use of Estimates
The preparation of financial statements in conformity with generally accepted accounting
principles requires management to make estimates and assumptions. The estimates and
assumptions affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and disclosure of contingent assets
and liabilities at the date of the financial statements and the reported amount of revenues and
expenses during the reporting period. Actual results could differ from those estimates.
Cash and Cash Equivalents
The Foundation considers all highly liquid investments with an initial maturity of three months or
less when purchased to be cash equivalents.
Investments
Investments in marketable securities are stated at fair value and, to the extent that management
intends to hold such investments for more than one year, are classified as noncurrent assets. Gains
or losses that result from market fluctuations are recognized in the period in which such
fluctuations occur.
Equipment
Equipment, which consists of data processing equipment and furniture and fixtures, is carried at
cost and is depreciated on the straight-line method over three and five years, respectively.
Net Asset Categories
The Foundation reports information regarding its net assets and activities according to three classes
of net assets: unrestricted, temporarily restricted and permanently restricted.
• Unrestricted net assets are available for support of the Foundation's programs and
supporting services.
• Temporarily restricted net assets represent contributions whose use by the Foundation is
limited by donor-impose d restrictions. The restrictions can be fulfilled by incurring expenses
satisfying the restricted purposes.

• Permanently restricted net assets are restricted by the donor for investment in perpetuity.
These permanently restricted net assets consist of original corpus and an adjustment for
inflation in order to maintain the purchasing power of the scholarship funds.
The Foundation categorizes its financial position by fund based upon donor restrictions as follows:

General Fund-Resour ces are available for support of Foundation programs and
supporting services.
Masonic Model Student Assistance Fund-This fund was established by the Grand Lodge

to provide financial support to ongoing programs aimed at assisting students in
furthering their academic careers. All amounts in the fund are donor-restrict ed
specifically for use in these programs.

Scholarship Funds
Amaranth Fund- Resources are restricted by a trust agreement with the Amaranth

Homes of California. The agreement specifies that principal is to be invested and the
income is to be used to provide educational grants to women under age 21. Net assets
of $453,403 are restricted.

Wade-Amaranth Fund-This fund was established by a bequest from W.O. Wade.
Income from the fund is to be expended for scholarships and other like purposes for
female students seeking degrees from educational institutions in California. Net
assets of $1,124,013 are restricted.
F.M. Robinson Memorial Fund-This fund was established by contributions from
Mrs. F.M. Ropinson. The principal of the fund cannot be expended. Income from the
fund is to be expended for scholarships. Net assets of $73,939 are restricted

Harry Walker Lister Scholarship Fund-This fund was established from a

contribution of a variable appreciable life insurance policy. The policy was redeemed
during 1988. The principal of the fund cannot be expended. The income of the fund
can only be used to fund scholarships. Net assets of $355,186 are restricted.

Starr King Lodge No. 344 Scholarship Fund-This fund was established by the Starr

Collection of Books and Nonvaluable Contributions

California Masonic Memorial Temple (the Temple) is a nonprofit organization. According to the
Articles of Incorporation, income from the Temple, less operating expenses and reserves, is to be
transferred to the Endowment Fund of Masonic Homes of California (Masonic Homes) and/ or the
California Masonic Foundation (the Foundation). The amount and proportions of such
distributions are at the sole discretion of the Board of Trustees.

The Temple library contains a book collection of approximately 10,000 volumes. The collection
includes approximately 8,500 works on Masonic and related philosophic topics and nearly 1,500
non-Masonic volumes, including historical, religious, scientific, political and biographical works.
Fewer than 50 works in the collection could be considered rare. The Temple museum contains
donated items such as works of art and historical treasures contributed by members of the Free and
Accepted Masons of California. The Temple museum collection contains donated items from the
membership of The Masonic Fraternity in California and elsewhere. Artifacts in the collection
include works of art, Masonic regalia and numerous historical pieces. The Temple does not
recognize books and nonvaluable contributions in its financial statements. The Temple does not
recognize these assets as contributions, as they are protected and preserved, held for public
exhibition and subject to an organizational policy that requires proceeds from the sale of collection
items to be used to acquire other items for collections. Accessions and deaccessions of books and
nonvaluable contributions during 1999 and 1998 were not significant.

Use of Estimates

Revenue Recognition

The preparation of financial statements in conformity with generally accepted accounting
principles requires management to make estimates and assumptions. These estimates and
assumptions affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and disclosure of contingent assets
and liabilities at the date of the financial statements and the reported amount of revenues and
expenses during the reporting period. Actual results could differ from those estimates.

Contributions are recognized when received or unconditionally pledged.

1. ORGANIZATION AND SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:
Organization

Cash and Cash Equivalents
The Temple considers all highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less
when purchased to be cash equivalents.
Investments
Investments in marketable securities are stated at estimated fair value based on quoted market
prices. Investments received through gifts are recorded at estimated fair market value at the date
of donation.

Functional Expenses Allocations

Expenses, such as depreciation, supplies, travel, personnel and occupancy costs, are allocated
among program servic:p and general and administrative services classifications on the basis of
estimates made by the Temple's management.
Tax-Exempt Status
The Temple is a nonprofit corporation as described in Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue
Code and has been granted tax-exempt status by the Interrtal Revenue Service and the California
Franchise Tax Board. As discussed in Note 5, the Temple is subject to certain federal excise taxes.

4. OPERATING LEASES:
Nob Hill has an operating lease with the Temple, expiring June 30, 2003, under which Nob Hill
manages the Temple auditorium, exhibit hall, parking garage and various rental properties. Under
the terms of the lease, Nob Hill is required to pay rent equal to 90 percent of the gross rental

141

revenues in excess of $860,000 per year, adjusted annually for inflation, until Nob Hill has paid
$240,000, after which payment shall be one-third of the remaining gross rental revenues.
Beginning in 1998, the aggregate rent calculated under this formula is subject to a limit that
increases with inflation. The aggregate rent for the year ended June 30, 1999, is limited to $415,000.
For the year ended June 30, 1999, adjusted gross rental revenues, as defined in the lease agreement.
were $1,923,822, which generated $415,000 in lease revenue to the Temple. For the year ended
June 30, 1998, adjusted gross rental revenues, as defined in the lease agreement. were $2,153,878,
which generated $400,000 in lease revenue to the Temple.
5. FEDERAL EXCISE TAXES:

In accordance with applicable tax provisions, the Temple is classified as a private foundation and is
subject to an excise tax on net investment income, including realized gains. Accordingly, federal
excise taxes have been recognized in the amount of $10,476 during 1999 and $21,671during1998.
6. RELATED-PARTYTRAN SACI10NS:
The Temple leases the Temple auditorium. exhibit hall, parking garage and various rental
properties to Nob Hill (see Note 4).
The Grand Lodge provides general and administrative support to the Temple, for which it is
reimbursed through an allocation of certain expenses. The allocations for the years ended June 30,
1999 and 1998, were $15,419 and 514,750, respectively.

on these financial statements based on our audits.
We conducted our audits in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those
standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement An audit includes examining,
on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An
audit also includes assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by
management. as well as evaluating the overall financial statement presentation. We believe that
our audits provide a reasonable basis for our opinion.
In our opinion. the financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material respects, the
financial p<JSition of Nob Hill Masonic Management. Inc. as of June 30, 1999 and 1998, and the

accumulated plan benefits earned by the participants to reflect the time value of money (through
discounts for interest) and the probability of payment (by means of documents such as for death,
disability, withdrawal or retirement) between the valuation date and the expected date of payment.

APPENDIXE

GRAND LODGE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

171

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY

Most Worshipful, and Brethren:
This is my eighth report to you as Grand Secretary. The Grand Master has
asked me to be very brief because there is so much legislation to consider. I will
therefore only cover the highlights in this report.
The membership statistics continue to show a decline in the total number
of Master Masons. In 1998 we had 98,526 Master Masons on the rolls as of June
30, and this year we have 94,693. That's the bad news. The good news is that the
number of Entered Apprentices initiated during 1998/1999 increased once more
over the previous year. Although the increase was modest, it was an increase - for
the second year in a row. If this trend continues, and grows stronger, our
membership problems are at least being addressed in a positive manner.
In addition, the number of suspensions for "non-payment of dues"
decreased from l, 702 to 1,364 in 1999. While that is still too many, again, the
trend is in the right direction.
This year the Membership Department took on a new responsibility with
the beginning of a new Homes Endowment Fund program. The Grand Lodge
Office now records all contributions individually in the database, increasing the
value of the information to the Masonic Homes as well as to Grand Lodge. This
new responsibility has been taken in stride by our staff members, and I am pleased
to report to you that it is going well.
Finally, the Grand Master this year extended recognition to both factions
within the Grand Lodge of Portugal. Both the so-called "Regular Grand Lodge of
Portugal" and the I' Regular - Legal Grand Lodge of Portugal" claimed to be the
legitimate government of that Grand Lodge. The Grand Master recognized both
groups until the situation could sort itself out. Our recognition of the Grand Lodge
of Portugal continues, and when it is clear who the responsible leaders are, we will
no doubt once more recognize only one Grand Master in that Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
John L. Cooper III, Grand Secretary

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER

Most Worshipful, Brethren:
The Ritual Committee Report for 1999 will be very brief. The
performance of our Ritual continues to be a major concern. We are still plagued by
lack of officers in all too many of our lodges, and "re-treads" are much too
common. However, attendance at the Grand Lecturer's Seminars continues to be
very good. Perhaps the inspiration from these seminars will spread to the lodges
and encourage better performance of all the Ritual.
Respectfully submitted,
Ulysses G. Patropulos, Grand Lecturer

GRAND CHAPLAIN'S MESSAGE
Sean N. Foran, Grand Chaplain

"The Light of God in the Soul of Man"
Never in history have ordinary men and women needed Divinely generated
light more than in these days. Society has become fragmented, as the cohesive
strength of religious faith, moral values, respect for law, patriotism and family unity
have become undermined.
Religious, moral, political and personal standards have lost much of the
respect, persuasiveness and authority that they once enjoyed. The exploiter who by
the tricks-of-the-trade amasses his millions overnight. The political leaders and the
supposed servants of the people in the government often utilize their office for the
·
perpetuation and advancement of their own careers.
Greed and self-interest seem to motivate the leadership of many
organizations. Pleasure-seeking and self-gratification, increasingly poison
relationships.
The confusion of modem life, the use of supposedly noble aims to mask
evil motives, the subversion oflanguageto propaganda, the perversion of moral and
religious values to serve immoral ends has caused the Darkness of distrust to
permeate society.
It is the great tragedy in the life of many people that they so entirely
devote themselves to the body's needs that they forget, or neglect the spirit's needs.
Giving themselves up to the search for things, for temporalities, they leave the
divinest cravings in them to go unsatisfied; as a result, they become materialistic,
self-centered, vain, greedy and animalistic. God becomes unreal, and the future life
uncertain; and they even fall into the fatal habit of making such goodness, truth and
beauty, as they do ftnd in themselves or others, into a mere means to an end. Such
a persons whole life revolves about himself; he becomes his own world and his own
God, and out of such a state grow the fears, doubts, superstitions, quarrelings,
graspings, prejudices, envyings and hatreds, which so often make life a mere
scramble after the things of self. In other words, the body is set at the center of
existence so that all the man's life is made up oftemporalities.
The one remedy for this condition is to change the center of gravity so that
the spirit is master and the body is servant, so that search is made for the eternal
things instead of wholly for the things that pass away.
The Symbols of Masonry were old, perhaps, when the Pyramids were new.
The working tools of the Craft antedate the time when Jesus toiled at a carpenter's
bench in Nazareth. Rich with the spoils of time, the language of the Masonic Ritual
sounds quaint to modem ears.
Masonry is an organiution of principles, of principles drawn from the
highest sources ofhuman reason and Divine revelation, of principles in their nature
profoundly philosophical, and in their practical exhibition and influence, of untold
value to the family of man. The right angles, the squares, the circles, and the
triangles, are but the visible casements that conceal the spirit within.

201

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

In whom do you put your trust? In God. Here brethren, is the foundation
of Masonry. The candidate for initiation is met at the threshold and nothing but a
declaration of his firm reliance upon the Almighty God can ensure his admission.
No excellence of reputation, no influence of wealth or station, can avail in lieu of
faith in the true and living God.
Look again, brethren, to the altar. There you can behold the sacred
writings spread out, like a broad luminary, casting its bright light over a dark and
gloomy earth. This is our foundation; we are indeed based upon the eternal rock
of truth; and neither the treachery or baseness of man, nor even the corroding lapse
of years shall weaken our hope, nor quench the fire that bums upon our sacred altar.
Faith its foundation, Righteousness its cornerstone, Strength and Wisdom
its walls, Beauty its form and fashion, Brotherly Love its clasped arches, Reverence
its roof, the Bible its altar light, Mysticism its music, Charity its incense,
Fellowship and Relief its ritual.
Its symbols half-revealing and half-concealing a Truth too elusive for
words, too vast for dogma, and too bright for eyes unveiled, and only hinted to us,
until we are ready and worthy to behold it, with other and clearer eyes than now we
know.
If the rituals and ceremonials of the lodge room constituted the whole of
Masonry, then there is a phenomenon connected with its history and its reception
among men that cannot be explained by any known laws of human action. What
is the charm of it, the mystical lure and might of it, which time cannot wither or
custom stale? That men of all creeds and professions, of all stations and conditions
in society, the prince ofnoble birth and the peasant of humble pretensions, that the
men of every land and language and nation under heaven should all be pleased and
gratified with Masonry, should esteem it a distinguished honor to be permitted to
associate in our Lodges, take part in our labors, and be considered a brother among
us; and yet that Masonry is nothing but rituals and ceremony, an empty show, is
certainly one of the most singular features in the philosophy of man. And then that
all these various classes of men should sustain and patronize an institution,
consisting of mere shadows, for centuries, and love it the better, the more they
know of it, is something that human reason cannot account for, and credulity itself
will not believe.
In the social world, Masonry has wielded an influence that perhaps no
other association ever did. Avoiding a conflict with governments and laws, and
laying down a few simple and vastly important doctrines, free from sectarianism,
and of universal application; making morality her motto, and exacting friendship
and brotherly love among her followers, she has travelled through the earth as a
messenger of good.
There is something in her laws, or her rituals, or her instructions, and I can
scarcely tell what it is, that produces feelings of warm friendship and devoted
kindness between men who would otherwise remain entire strangers to each other.
There is something of the kind, I have often experienced, when a stranger among
strangers. It is mysterious and silent in its workings, but powerful in its results. It
breaks down the barrier of cold, formal etiquette, clasps hand in hand, and brings
heart to heart as though friendship had been formed and affection strengthened by
the acquaintance of years.

No matter what degree in Masonry is being exemp!ified, ~e know exactly
what is coming. We can climb, without a candle, the ancient sta1rway that leads
from the lowly Entered Apprentice to the lofty degree of Master Mason. Before ~e
work our way in, we can visualize the "old familiar faces" of the bre~en who will
greet us in the lodge roo!D. Vfe can name! almost t~ am~, the faithful s~dbys
who will be there. Yet, in spite of crowding cares! in spite. of a world that is !OO
much with us, we find ourselves, on lodgenight, with a tug in our hearts, meeting
upon the level and parting upon the square.
Rich with the spoils of fraternal sentimen~ that frugall~ furnished lodge
room has become the fireside of a thousand chenshed memones. Out of ~uch
homely humdrum associations as these, out of such commonplace matenals,
Masom). weaves a spell that holds our heartstrings taut, our loyalty true, when other
ties have been severed by the sharp ways of the world. There is something unique
in Masonry, a tie unlike any other, ~itingmen of all ranks, ~p~s, temperaments
into a closely-knit fellowship; something deep and tender. We sit in lodge together,
each knowing exactly what will C?I?e next; we meet upon the l~v~l and part upon
the square, old and simple and fam1har symbols, and somehow a tie is woven. Here
a little, there a little, line upon line, it braids a cabletow that is soft as a baby's first
caress, yet stronger than cables of steel.
What is this bond which the Truculent Three cannot break, and only death
itself can sever? Perhaps it is near the truth to say that it is a strand from the great
golden cabletow of God, running from heart to heart; a cabletow whose strands
might be named brotherly love, relief, truth.
The lesson of the First Degree, is to set man free from ignorance,
superstition and fear; "he is bound to a stronger tie." He is found wo!1hy to be free,
only in the sense and to the degree that he undertakes to control himself, ~d he
voluntarily assum~ the obligation and undertakes the work. He learns morahty and
charity, two things always to be kept together. That he should be a good m~ an~
true. The first emblem of Masonry which is presented to the entered app~ntice is
the lambskin apron, which is at once an embl~m of. inn.ocence and punty,_ and

and appetites. If counted worthy, we pass, in ~e Second. ~e~ee, out of you~ into

of Eternity living in time. That man is a Builde~ of a Temple, a ~llgnm in ques~ of

He is, first, a builder, taking the rough stones of th~ wor!d and. sha~mg the!D m!o

and d~ath, t~ward the East, the place of sunrise and life; a pilgrimage of the soul,
affected, at least in this state of its journey, in the sandals of Human Nature, a long,
weary road. He is, finally, if he be worthy, a finder of the greatest secret, that of
eternal life.
I declare to you unequivocally that _back of all the symbo!i~al in
Freemasonry lies the actual, the real, .the subs~t1al and the true; ~d that it is the
real that gives life and light and meaning to the ideal and the symbohcal. That back
and beyond the reputed Master ~ere is the real M~ter; tha! back of! beyond and

of which the Speculative is only a hint, a symbol, an outer form.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

One group of our activities has reference always to the body. We work to
earn money so that we may clothe, and feed, and shelter the body; if we seek
pleasure it is to please the same body; if we desire possessions it is that the wants
and needs of the body may be satisfied.
But there is in each of us another set of activities which have reference to
the spirit. By nature, of its very nature, man's spirit is a thing that seeks Goodness,
Truth and Beauty. Just as food is the satisfaction of the stomach's appetiteso are
these the satisfaction of the spirit's cravings. We can call it soul, a divine spark or
what you will, which even now is not concerned with time or space, but exists
above outside them. This God like thing in us need not wait for death to make it
Eternal; it is Eternal now.
We learn in the Third Degree that Freemasonry is a vision of a living
Temple - noble, stately, sheltering all the holy things of humanity, slowly rising in
the midst of the ages; a Temple building and built upon, each workman not only a
builder, but himself a living stone, foursquare and finely wrought, to be built into
the whole. Such must be our insight and faith that we are fellow-workers with the
eternal Creative God, and therefore made to be not only Builders, but Brothers,
made to share the large innocence of nature, and the unfailing love of God, who
cares more for a brother than for all possessions.
When our center of gravity changes so that the spirit is master and the
body is servant, so that search is made for the eternal things instead of wholly for
the things that pass away. When this occurs, selfishness, envy and materialism
vanish; the soul becomes the.great reality; God draws very near and becomes very
certain; the perspective oflife is changed and its scale of values is reversed. To be
honorable and true, to love others, to live in pity, charity, and kindliness, to know
eternity as present and the present existence is a brief place of an endless life, all
this becomes for such a man the great ideal toward which all his energies are bent.
Loss and disease may be serious but they are not fatal.
He who finds the "Light of God in the Soul of Man" is victorious always.
If he is betrayed by the friends in whom he trusted, waylaid by ruffians,
put to death, and thrown into an unmarked grave, heis not defeated or destroyed;
the God-like spirit within him, dedicated to the Eternal Values, raises him up from
the level of death to the perpendicular of the life that even now is eternal.

GRAND ORATION

Melvyn B. Stein, Grand Orator
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren:
"The Choir Isn't Singing"
As the butt of many attorney jokes, I will try to be mindful of the statement
of Thomas Jefferson who said, "It is the trade oflawyers to question everything, to
give nothing, and to talk by the hour." Others, in referring to lawyers statements
have said, "We heard him, but what did he say?"
Hopefully, this afternoon some questions will be raised and your thoughts
stimulated over a short period of time at the conclusion of which you may answer,
"I will join the choir."
In the early l 700's Masonry was primarily composed of men of means and
political power. Younger men, such as George Washington, who wanted to move
up into a higher social-economic level would join our Fraternity in hope of greater
achievement. Masons were visible in public life and virtue was their cornerstone.
From the building of King Solomon's Temple, Masonry has used the
working tools of the stone mason and mixed them with a metaphorical journey from
darkness to light in which all mankind could live in peace and harmony.
The true history of Masonry prior to the Grand Lodge in 1717 is clouded.
Masonic tradition is portrayed no more eloquently than in the DeMolay Degree and
its lesson of refusal by Jacques DeMolay to submit to tyranny and his refusal to
accept the bondage of men to a lack of free thought. In the Third Degree, we are
taught that the Master's word was lost. Further study reveals that the true word is
contained within our own hearts and minds.
Where and how does all of this fit within our social-economic fast-paced,
high-tech, communication driven, televised internet society?
While we in this land of freedom pay little heed to the Masonic principles
that were once revolutionary, of the freedom of thought and the right to express that
thought, it remains a goal sought by many in countries throughout the world. It still
remains a primary task of Masonry to promulgate these principles. Masonry has
the overriding responsibility to assure the survival of such free thought and
expression.
Masonry and the academic community is the first to be attacked by the
dictator who cannot condone the freedom of man espoused by Masonry. From the
days of the inquisition to the days of Hitler's Germany and the closure of Masonic
Lodges throughout the then conquered Europe, the sign of the yellow poppy was
the only emblem of living free thought. The eastern European countries and the
Union of Soviet Socialist Republic purged all Masons from the era of Stalin to the
fall of the Berlin Wall. Today, the hunger for Masonic philosophy has caused it to
again emerge in places like Hungary, Cuchoslovakia, Poland, Romania and as well
as in South America.
In this country, we are the bastion for Freemasonry. Even in England the
Lord Chancellor has decreed that those seeking government positions should list

207

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

their Masonic membership on their application. This alone should cause us grave
concern. Our own California judicial council has asked California Judges who
were members of the Masonic Fraternity, what they intended to do in light of the
fact that women were not permitted to enter the craft, thereby constituting
discrimination. Some Judges have not returned to our Lodges and their activities
have diminished. There are some well known exceptions.
While Masonic principles have remained steadfast, we hear all around us
the call for change, particularly in light of declining membership which is
interposed with the question of the relevance of Masonry in today's society.
At one time the first three degrees of Masonry were committed to memory
from mouth to ear without a cypher ritual book and usually required the candidates'
coach to explain the meaning to the novitiate of that which was being memorized.
Now, most of our candidates' coaches are reduced to assisting a candidate
memorize an obligation and certain grips and words; but the lessons taught by the
degrees are not required to be known or learned by the candidate, and subsequently,
may be lost except to the studious.
When a man has completed his first, second or third degree and he walks
out of that Lodge room (sometimes to infrequently return) is it clear to him what we
have said and done? Does the novitiate leave confused? Does he understand the
allegories and hidden meanings? Are we imparting useful knowledge and a way
of life by which that candidate can pattern his own life? Some jurisdictions have
addressed this problem, not by memorization, but by open booklet examinations
after each degree.
Only a small portion of our obligation has been adopted by the "promise
keepers groups" which has drawn men in large numbers to stadiums. Masonry has
much more to offer. By our eloquent verbiage, do we communicate directly to the
candidate or do we even communicate to the general public that which we have
been taught or that which we would teach?
It has been said that possibly Masonry has lost the baby boomer
generation. This ship has not yet gone down like the Titanic. It is the largest
demographic group of men and the greatest potential source of Masonic candidates.
We speak of2 l year olds as active members. This group still faces a tough period
of finding a job and keeping it, trying to make a living, getting married, raising
children and seeking some form of stability within a family structure. On the other
hand, the baby boomer generation has attained stability in their income and
employment, their children are over 16 and are looking beyond mom and dad, and
more free time is available to them. These men in their fifties are looking for
something beyond the television and are not ready to simplyput on their slippers,
sit in a rocking chair and eat T.V. dinners. These men are looking for something
to associate with that has meaning, substance, creates a group of social friends and
provides service to the community. These are the very attributes that Masonry has
to offer. These men, however, are still time conscious and demand to easily
understand what it is that we or other similar groups have to teach or to offer them.
As a child, I still recall Dr. Seuss and his Horton the Elephant who said,
"I said what I meant and I meant what I said ..." Masonry must learn to impart our
concepts clearly and concisely.
Masons do not need to sell Masonry. Masonry can sell itself when it is
clearly stated. A movie popular in the last few years stood for the principle that if

you build a stadium (or in our case a great Fraternity),just wait, and they will come.
In the case of Masonry, only a handful know that the stadium (or Fraternity) has
been built. In the case of potential members Masonry is generally believed to be
more appropriate for their fathers or grandfathers than for themselves. We must,
therefore, actively promote a shared vision by a program of outreach to the
community and let the general public become aware of our presence among them
and what it is that Masonry stands for. Our stadium has been erected from the
cement offellowship and charity through individual and community service and the
virtues which form the cement of peace and harmony among all men.
California Masonry requires an attitude adjustment. Each ofus has heard
of the loss of membership and where our Fraternity may be in 20 years. It is true
that all fraternal organizations as well as service organizations in the United States
are experiencing a decline in membership. We must approach those in our
community with a positive attitude or what we have to offer that can draw men
closer to us and cause them to join with us. We cannot accomplish our goals by an
attitude of seeking to ask a neighbor to join a dying organization. Who wants to ask
them to join a Lodge whose doors are likely to close? We must take the nonnegative, affirmative high road to our great stadium and the principles upon which
it is constructed.
Masonry is not in the 911t inning with 2 outs. Masonry still has the greatest
and largest Fraternity the world has ever known with precepts that no man can fault
with the Holy Writings as the rule and guide of our faith. A truly Masonic way of
life is a minister's dream to build a congregation. Don't sell Masonry short, my
brethren.
Masonry in California is not sitting on its hands.
The Grand Lodge of California, through its California Masonic
Foundation, provided over $875,000 in scholarships actually paid between May and
June of 1999. The students emanated from approximately 81 different California
communities. No Masonic affiliation was required.
Over $450,000 was provided this year to almost 800 elementary and
middle school teachers and administrators for the purpose of a free two night, three
day training session at the Masonic Home in Covina, where they were taught to
recognize children at risk due to alcohol, drugs or child abuse. More importantly,
the program provides a solution as to what to do once a problem is recognized. No
Masonic affiliation is required.
The California Scottish Rite Foundation supports 13 Childhood Language
Disorders Clinics at a cost just last year alone of over 1.6 million dollars. Since the
first clinic was created in 1970, here in San Francisco, approximately 750,000 child
visits have occurred at a cost of approximately $19 million dollars. No Masonic
affiliation is required.
The California Scottish Rite Foundation also provides college scholarships
as well as scholarships on the graduate level. Last year $130,000 was so provided.
The Knight Templars and York Rite Bodies have provided hundreds of
thousands of dollars for eye care, for mental disorders and for all types of treatment
for which no Masonic affiliation is required.
The Shrine provides over 1.3 million dollars 31:~ forthe benefit of the
22 Shriner' s Hospitals for Children. There are no insurance clerks or cash registers

as all services are provided at no charge. No Masonic affiliation is required.
The California Masonic Foundation Child ID Program provides
identification and a photograph of children for the assistance of their parents and
law.enforcement should they become lost or missing.
Substantial funds, clothing and toys are provided by many Masonic
concordant bodies vigorously supported by our ladies.
On a community level, one need only to refer to our publication The
California Freemason underthe heading of"Freemasonry Serving the Community"
and read of the thousands of dollars provided for scholarships, schools and
community charities.
Masonry certainly is not sitting on its hands. It is vibrant and contributing
heavily to the needs of our society and our state.
We must inform the community of our efforts taken on their behalf. The
membership has continually looked to the Grand Lodge for their only solution, and
that somehow our San Francisco headquarters should magically emit a continuous
light beam of communication to all citizens within our state.
This leads to what a Mason recently asked when he heard a presentation
extolling the many attributes of Masonry and its public service, "Why are you
preaching to the choir?" There is an answer for him - Because the choir isn't
singing.
There are over 94,000 California Masons. What better means ofspreading
information throughout the state could any group or organization have than a choir
of94,000. All 94,000 strong need to start singing the praises of what we are doing
for the benefit of our communities without any requirement of Masonic
relationship.
Our stadium is planted firmly throughout this state of California, and they
will come if you and all of our brother Masons and all members of our concordant
bodies will join the choir, and all 94,000 sing loudly and clearly to let all know who
we are, what we are and what Masonry is doing in service to mankind. So mote it
be!

Grand Master Nahin's Recommendation No. 1
Repeals Inspectors Tenure

The wisdom and experience of all who are a part of our Grand Lodge are
very important. We should, at all times, endeavor to strengthen our Jurisdiction.
A prudent approach would and should be to build and benefit from our strengths
and address our weaknesses. This appertains not only to procedures and established
practices but to individuals as well. A major concern, within our structure, is that
of the position of Inspector. This appointed position requires that the brother not
only be duly qualified but also devote an enormous amount of personal time. Much
talent exists within our Jurisdiction, but experience proves that talent alone does not
produce a desirable Inspector. An effective Inspector must commit himself to a
great amount of personal time and dedication. Many are willing to serve as an
Inspector, but few are willing or able to commit the personal dedication and time
that is needed. I believe that tenure of an Inspector should be based upon a periodic
evaluation to determine the need for change or for reappointment. Change is
definitely necessary, from time to time, and should be made as required. Those that
demonstrate wisdom, talent and commitment of time should be given serious
consideration for reappointment, regardless of time served. Time and experience
have produced the most effective Inspectors. Often times, in our challenges of
today, it is very difficult to find individuals with these desired qualities, especially
the commitment of personal time, which is so necessary.
I believe that the tenure of an Inspector's appointment or reappointment
be at the discretion of the Grand Master and that the nine-year limitation should be
discontinued.
Ifyou adopt this recommendation, Section 4010 of the California Masonic
Code will be amended to read as follows:
§4010. APPOINTMENT.
The Grand Master shall divide the Jurisdiction into districts, and
shall appoint for each district an Inspector, who shall be a Past
Master of this Jurisdiction, and who shall, before entering upon
his duties, produce a certificate from the Grand Lecturer or an
Assistant Grand Lecturer that he is proficient in the work and
lectures adopted by the Grand Lodge and is qualified to act as
Inspector. Each Inspector shall serve for a term of one year,
commencing on January 1 following the Grand Master's
installation and terminating on December 31 of the same year.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master's Recommendation No. 1 seeks to remove the nine (9) year
limit on the term of Inspectors.
Section 4010 of the California Masonic Code currently allows the Grand
Master to reappoint an Inspector for the good of the Craft.
The established policy was created to permit more leadership participation
within the Grand Lodge.
If approved, this could possibly create an inconsistency within the Grand
Lodge, as committeemen would still be limited to nine (9) years.
This Recommendation is not consistent with Grand Lodge policy and
general purposes.

Grand Master Nahin's Recommendation No. 2
Changes Name of Masonic Homes Endowment Board
to Committee and Increases Membership to Not More than 50 Members
We are greatly indebted to the group of Masons in California who have
served on what we now call the "Masonic Homes Endowment Board". They have
gone out to the Lodges and spoken on behalf of the great work that our Masonic
Homes are doing for the adults and for children at our two locations in Union City
and in Covina. They have done great things in raising monies for our Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund so that perpetually we will have the funds to help those
needy and wonderful kids in Covina and the venerable and respected and loved
senior citizens who occupy the premises at Union City and at Covina. We can
never thank them enough.
However it seems to me that the term "Masonic Homes Endowment
Board" is a misnomer. A Board is a policy making and decision making body. The
Homes Endowment Board on the other hand is charged with assisting the Masonic
Homes in raising funds from the Lodges, to increase the awareness of the benefits
provided by the Homes and to encourage annual financial support from all
California Masons. It has no policy making or decision making duties or
responsibilities.
Additionally, restructuring it as a Standing Committee, instead of a
Constitutional Board, signifies the continued importance of its purpose.
Additionally, I would recommend that the Masonic Homes Endowment
Committee be composed ofat least 15 but not more than 50 members so that the
Committee will have added flexibility to be more efficient and effective in reaching
Lodges under its jurisdiction with such geographic diversity. This larger number
of members than the 35 now on the Committee would be more cost effective
because members will then be less likely to drive great distances and will be less
likely to incur additional costs such as hotel accommodations.
A Grand Lodge Committee is responsible for implementing the direction
of the Grand Lodge in its programs. That is clearly the function of the Masonic
Homes Endowment Board. Renamingit a Committee will clarify its purpose and

GRAND LOOOE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

213

tit the overall purpose for which it is established. Committees carry out policies,
be it of the Grand Lodge or of the Grand Master. The Homes Endowment Board
carries out policy and does it well but it should be named a Committee, not a Board.

Recommendation ADOPTED.

Grand Master Nahin's Recommendation No. 3
Eliminates the Deputy Grand Master and
Junior Grand Warden as Ex-officio Members
of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
At present the California Masonic Code provides that the Junior Grand
Warden, Senior Grand Warden and Deputy Grand Master will sit as Trustees of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple and as Trustees of the Masonic Homes of
California and that the Deputy Grand Master shall sit as a memberofthe California
Masonic Foundation. The Bylaws ofNob Hill Management Company provide that
the Junior Grand Warden shall sit as a member of that corporation's Board of
Directors.
In view of the increased demands of time upon the Elective Progressive
Line, including a new responsibility as members of a five year Research and
Planning Committee, I have discussed the need for having three representatives as
members of the California Masonic Memorial Temple with my Executive
Committee (who are presently most affected) and with the leadership of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple. I have determined that only one officer of
the Elective Progressive Line would be necessary to establish a proper
understanding and participation in the establishment and performance of policies
of that organization with reporting capabilities to the Grand Master. I therefore
believe that one officer of the Progressive Elective Line would be a sufficient and
complete representation on the Board by the Grand Lodge Elective Line. I have
also determined that, like the Nob Hill Management and the Foundation, only one
Elective Line Officer should serve on Board of Directors of the California Masonic
Memorial Temple.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section I 0020 of the California
Masonic Code will be amended to read as follows:

§10020. COMPOSITION OF BOARD.
The Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple shall
be nine in number. The Depttey Grand htmter, Senior Grand
Warden and Jtt11io1 Grand Wmden shall each be a Trustee
ex-officio. The other eight
Trustees shall be appointed by the
Grand Master for terms of three years each. The terms ofat least
two one thild of the appointed Trustees shall expire at the close
of each Annual Communication of Grand Lodge. When a
vacancy occurs, the appointee shall serve the remainder of the
unexpired term. The Grand Master may remove a Trustee at any
time, upon request of two-thirds of the Trustees, and appoint
another.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Grand Master Nahin proposes to remove the Deputy Grand Master and
Junior Grand Warden from the California Masonic Memorial Temple as ex-officio
members.
During the time that California Masonic Memorial Temple and Nob Hill
were formulating their future plans as well as their plans for the Library and
Museum, it was felt that the presence of the Junior Grand Warden, Senior Grand
Warden and Deputy Grand Master would enhance their understanding of the inner
workings of the Temple. Now that California Masonic Memorial Temple and Nob
Hill have made the transition into a very well run business, this visibility is no
longer necessary. We can and should go back to just having the Senior Grand
Warden serve as ex-officio member on the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
This recommendation is consistent with the Grand Lodge policy and
general purposes.
Recommendation ADOPTED.
Grand Master Nahin's Recommendation No. 4
Makes Offices of Grand Secretary, Grand Treasurer and
Grand Lecturer Appointive Rather than Elective

At present our California Masonic Code provides for the election of seven
officers each year: the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Senior Grand Warden,
Junior Grand Warden, Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary and Grand Lecturer. Only
four of those are progressive: the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Senior
Grand Warden and Junior Grand Warden. The other three, Grand Treasurer, Grand
Secretary and Grand Lecturer, serve for periods of one year and are generally
reelected to their present positions. We applaud the wonderful work, devotion and
loyalty of the Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary and Grand Lecturer but are at a loss
to determine why these three Officers who are non-policy making officers of the
Grand Lodge should be elected and not appointed as they are in many other
jurisdictions. They serve a wonderful purpose in our Grand Lodge, and the present
occupants are and have been dedicated and devoted to the cause of Freemasonry
and to the policy of the Grand Lodge for many years. It is not my intention in
making the following recommendation to in any way suggest a desire or intent to
change the present occupants of the office, but to permit them, should they be
recommended each year by our Grand Lodge in accordance with the existing Grand
Lodge Law, to function as long as the Great Architect of us all will permit them to
function and as long as they desire to do so and as long as the Grand Lodge so sees
fit for them to do so.
It is my firm belief, however, in discussing this with Grand Masters of
other jurisdictions in the United States that the appointment of such officers is in
keeping with proper procedure and policy.

It is abundantly clear to any of us who sit in this room as active members
of the. Masonic !raternity and partic~larly of the Grand Lodge of California that
sufficient attention has not been and is not now being paid to the education of our
candidates for the Ent~red_Apprentice, Fellowcraft or Master Mason Degrees. We
know that such education is necessary, or rather that it is vital if we are to maintain
our position in the State as a premiere fraternal organization. We cannot just make
Masons ~y ~onferring the rituals or having a ritualistic proficiency of whatever kind
or descnptton. Men who become members of our Craft must know and must
understand what it is they are joining, what has happened to our fraternity before
and.what may_ happen to our fraternity in the future. They can do that only by
having education.

result~d in ehmina.t1on of an~ re9u1rement other than memorization of a part of the
proficiency catechism, resulting in newly-made Masons who haven't been informed
of Masonic history or Masonic philosophy or Masonic law.
Masonic information for candidates is essential and desirable because:
Each candidate for Freemasonry should be knowledgeable as to

for a period of not less than one year.

a clearly written procedure with instructions and sample answers to be distributed
to each Lodge. This will assure consistent implementation of this addition to the
candidate proficiencies and appropriate monitoring ofits use and value. (They shall
also provide that these pamphlets and questions and the procedure and sample
answers be made available on the Internet.)

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Nahin is correct in his observation that there has been little
effort expended in educating our new candidates with regard to the history,
philosophy, and relevancy of Masonry. This situation was further aggravated by
the reduction in the proficiency requirement. While Section 6160 of our Masonic
Code charges the Education Committee to promote Masonic education, this effort
is largely directed at lodges or other groups, not at individuals.
It is Most Worshipful Nahin' s proposal that we require Masonic education
for all new Masons while still avoiding rote memorization. There is precedent for
written examinations. Sections 25070C, 25080C, and 25090C of the California
Masonic Code mandate that incoming Masters and Wardens be proficient with the
Masonic Code; open-book, written examinations have been employed to fulfill that
requirement for many years.
It is not the"intent of Masonry simply to have members pay dues and go
to social events. Masonry espouses a value system that is often neglected in our
current society. The dissemination, support, and practice of our value system are
the things that differentiate us from other social or service organizations. A
promulgation of the Masonic value system is essential to society as a whole, and
we need to conduct it whenever and wherever we can. An open-book examination
will allow the candidate to learn about Masonry, including its values, and to discuss
this material freely with his family and friends. The process may even produce
more enthusiastic participation by the candidate and increased numbers of
membership requests from his acquaintances.
The proposal is consistent with our current policies and purposes.
Recommendation CARRIED-OVER.

be required at that time.

of this Grand Lodge.

1998 ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
Grand Master Wordlow's Recommendation No. 1
Financial Accountability for Lodges
Financial accountability and financial integrity are irnportantto our lodges,
and to the Grand Lodge of California. The reputation of all lodges can be damaged
by the lack of accountability and financial integrity by one lodge, and to protect the
reputation of the Craft in general is a responsibility of the Grand Lodge of
California.
Lodges with sound financial practices always have a budget, and use the
budget as a guideline for the making of expenditures during the year. In addition,
our present Masonic law, as well as good financial practices, require the approval
of expenditures by vote of the lodge. However, the present law does not require the
adoption of a budget by the lodge, and does not require any standardized procedures
for presenting expenditures for approval to the lodge. Nor does it require
standardized forms for keeping track of such expenditures. This lack of uniformity
contributes to confusion in our lodges, and a greater difficulty for our officers who
are elected to manage the finances of the lodge than is necessary.
Accordingly, I am recommending that the following changes in our law
be adopted by Grand Lodge at the forthcoming Annual Communication:
•
•

•

•

All lodges should be required to adopt a budget at the first stated meeting
after the installation of the Master of the lodge.
All lodges should be required to vote to authorize expenditures, even
though budgeted in advance, so that the members know what financial
liabilities are being incurred by the lodge.
Lodges should be permitted to approve bills against the lodge only when
the bills are supported by proper documentation, such as an invoice or
receipt.
The semi-annual reports of the Secretary and the Treasurer should be
made on standard forms as approved by the Grand Master. And a copy of
those reports should be transmitted to the Grand Lodge.

As Grand Master I ask your support for this needed legislation.
If this recommendation is adopted, Section 210 I 0 of the California
Masonic Code will be amended to read~ as marked:

Resolution 98-06:
Defines Which Past Masters May Participate

The proponents of this Resolution seek to limit the Master Mason's proficiency to
the obligation, signs and modes of recognition of the third degree.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to define who can cast the collective Past
Masters' vote, and under what conditions it cannot be cast.

Annual Communication shortened the portion of the Candidate's Lecture in the
Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Degrees which the Mason is required to
memorize before advancing; and
WHEREAS, it is illogical to shorten the proficiencies in the first two
degrees without similarly shortening the proficiency in the third degree.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that a new Section 26345 be
added to the California Masonic Code to read as follows:

WHEREAS, there is confusion among the craft as to which Past Masters
are eligible to participate in the single vote accorded the Past Masters collectively
ofa Lodge;
WHEREAS, in the past some Past Masters not in attendance at an Annual
Communication have participated in voting on questions;
WHEREAS, in the past some Past Masters have participated in voting on
questions before those questions have been debated on Grand Lodge floor; and
WHEREAS, in the past some Past Masters, registered and in attendance
at an Annual Communication, have not been allowed to participate in the Past
Master's collective vote.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 620 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

232

§26345. PROFICIENCY IN THE MASTER MASON
DEGREE.
To obtain a Certificate of Proficiency in the Candidate's Lecture
of the Master Mason Degree. a Master Mason must give
satisfactory evidence. by examination in open Lodge. that he is
proficient and well qualified in the Master Mason degree. To
demonstrate such proficiency. a Master Mason shall only be
required to recite from memory the obligation of a Master
Mason, together with the signs and modes ofrecognition of that
degree.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents seek to limit the Master Mason's proficiency to the
obligation, signs and modes of recognition of the Third Degree.
Passage of this Resolution will achieve continuity among the required
proficiencies for the three degrees of Masonry and clarify the proficiency
requirements for the Master and Wardens. However, this Resolution will eliminate
the only formal admonition that a member receives concerning solicitation. Other
than that, this Resolution is consistent with Grand Lodge policy and general
purposes.

Resolution 98-08
Permits Stated Meetings in the Entered Apprentice Degree
The proponents of this Resolution seek to give each Lodge the option to hold its
Stated Meetings in the Entered Apprentice Degree.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M of California:
WHEREAS, as an historic perspective, it is acknowledged that, throughout
the formative years of Freemasonry, Entered Apprentices made up the bulk of the
membership in our Fraternity, and Fellow Crafts and Master Masons were rare;
WHEREAS, in the 1840's many Grand Lodges in the United States revised
their rules to require Lodges to hold Stated Meetings only in Lodges of Master
Masons, originally done to encourage all Masons to become Master Masons;
WHEREAS, this change eventually resulted in the exclusion of Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts from the core life of their Lodges, and contemporary
Masonic experience teaches us the importance of including Entered Apprentices
and Fellow Crafts whenever possible in the life and activities of the Lodge; and
WHEREAS, most Stated Meetings should be open to Entered Apprentices
and Fellow Crafts, with only balloting for candidates and election of officers being
reserved for Master Masons.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 16010 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

§16010. CONDITIONS FOR CONDUCTING AND
BUSINESS TO BE TRANSACTED.
A Lodge shall not be opened, nor shall any work be done or
business transacted, except by, or in the presence of, and under
the continual direction of the Master or the ranking Warden or
the Grand Master or his designated representative. All business,
except the examination of candidates in the lectures of the
Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees, the conferring of
the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees, and the
consideration of relief of a worthy Brother, shall be done in a
Lodge of Master Masons. unless the Lodge shall have exercised
the option as provided for elsewhere in this Code for conducting
such meetings in a Lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons. No

present except the conferring of degrees. The Tiler is present

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow each Past Master present
at Grand Lodge to vote.
At the present time, Section 620 D of the California Masonic Code allows
one vote collectively to all Past Masters present for each chartered Lodge.
Problems can arise when there is a difference of opinion among the Past
Masters present from a given Lodge. At times, all of those Past Masters are not
consulted regarding their opinion on some Resolutions.
This Resolution, as does Carry-Over Resolution No. 98-06, attempts to
address this problem, albeit with different solutions.
Our current balloting provides four votes to each Lodge, three of which are
cast by elected officials of that Lodge. This Resolution would change the
proportion ofballots that are cast by individual~ elected by th~ L~ge and those no~
so elected. Grand Lodge is ultimately responsible to all Cahforn1a Masons, and 1t
is appropriate to provide a majority of the ballots to individuals elected by tho~e
Masons. Our policy is to provide equal representation among all ~fthe L~ges m
California. If this Resolution is adopted, it could create a d1sproport1onate
representation of ballots by Lodges with large contingents of Past Masters.
This Resolution is not consistent with current Grand Lodge policy and
general purposes.

Resolution No. 99-0S
Requires Two or More Black Balls to Reject an Applicant
The proponents of this Resolution seek to require two or more black cubes to reject
an applicant for the degrees or for affiliation in the Lodge.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
WHEREAS Section 26190 of the California Masonic Code requires that
the election ofa candidate for the degrees of Masonry or for affiliation shall require
a unanimous vote; and
WHEREAS, potentially good applicants are being rejected by virtue of a
"black ball" vote cast by one biased, angry or unreasonable member who has acted
only based on his personal feelings; and
WHEREAS, we believe that this is an abuse of the ballot box.

Resolution No. 99-06
Counts Five Years Service in Armed Forces
of the United States During World War II
Toward the Golden Veterans Award
The proponents of this Resolution seek to include honorable military service in the
Armed Forces of the United States of America during World War II as partial
completion of the fifty years for awarding the Golden Veterans Award.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

WHEREAS, this resolution pertains only to those Master Masons who
served in the United States Armed Forces during World War 11 but, due to their
assignments of military duty at different locations in the world, did not join the
Masonic Order for numerous reasons. Some of the reasons would include 1) lack
of opportunity to apply for a petition, 2) the lack of knowledge of the proper
procedure for requesting a petition, 3) a duty station at a distant location where their
request would not have been heard, 4) a duty station at a place where action could
not have been taken. But these same Master Masons, our Brothers, upon returning
from a successful completion of the war, did in fact request said petition and
subsequently progressed on a timely basis to being raised to the Sublime Degree of
Master Mason; and
WHEREAS, the period for World War II is officially proclaimed by the
United States Government to be from December 7, 1941 to December 31, 1946, a
period of five years and 24 days; and
WHEREAS, during World War II there were 16,354,000 personnel on
active duty in the United States Armed Forces essential to the successful conduct
of the United States of America in military actions during World War II; and
WHEREAS, this change in awarding the Golden Veteran Award will
equalize the probability of World War II Veterans reaching the required fifty years
before his soul is commended to the Grand Architect of the Universe; and
WHEREAS, under this proposed change to Section 23150 of the
California Masonic Code, a brother who served and was discharged honorably in
the United States Armed Forces during the full period of World War II, could claim
and be granted five years and 24 days as good time toward the conferral of the
Golden Veterans Award. or any part served thereof and be granted respective, prorated good time towards said award.

Resolution No. 99-07
Pennits a Non-masonic Stenographic Reporter at a Masonic Trial
The proponents of this Resolution seek to pennit a non-Mason to act as a
stenographic reporter at a Masonic trial at the discretion of the Trial Master if no
disclosure of Masonic secrets would occur.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M ofCalifornia:
WHEREAS, Section 32290 of the California Masonic Code provides that
the Trial Master, in a trial of an individual Mason, may employ a duly accredited
stenographic reporter to transcribe the proceedings of such trial; and
WHEREAS, .Section 32290 also requires that any such stenographic
reporter be a Master Mason; and
WHEREAS, within the State of California, very few, if any, duly
accredited stenographic reporters are Master Masons; and
WHEREAS, it is frequently beneficial to have a verbatim stenographic
record of the trial of an individual Mason; and
WHEREAS, most trials of individual Masons do not involve disclosure of
any of the secrets of Freemasonry; and
WHEREAS, it would be beneficial to pennit a Trial Master the option and
discretion to have a stenographic reporter transcribe the proceedings if a reporter
who is a Master Mason is not available.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 32290 of the
California Masonic Code is amended as marked:

§32290. STENOGRAPHIC REPORTER.
At the option of the Trial Master, a duly accredited stenographic
reporter may be employed ifhc is a Master Mason. Whenever
reasonably possible, such reporter shall be a Master Mason. The
Trial Master shall, however. have the option to employ a
stenographic reporter who is not a Master Mason ifhe has first
reasonable concluded that the conduct of the proceedings is not
likely to involve the disclosure of any of the secrets of
Freemasonrv . If the reporter is a Master Mason, hHe shall
qualify upon his honor as a Master Mason before entering upon
his duty. The expenses of such reporter shall be borne by the
Lodge of which the accused is a member, if it is in this
Jurisdiction.

Resolution No. 99-08
Pennits Trial Master to Adjourn a Masonic Trial to a Specified Time
The proponents of .this Resolution seek to move all the Trial of an individual
Masons continuance provisions of Masonic Code into a single section and grant that
power to the Trial Master only.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M ofCalifornia:
WHEREAS, Article III of Part III (commencing with Section 32010) of
the California Masonic Code sets forth provisions dealing with the 'Trial of
Individual Mason'; and
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code currently contains two separate
and different sections dealing with requests for the continuance of trials of
individual Masons, with Section 32330 entitled 'CONTINUANCE' granting the
Trial Commissioners the right and authority to grant a continuance upon sufficient
showing by either party, while Section 32240 entitled 'AUTOMATIC
DISSOLUTION OF COMMISSION' pennits the Trial Master to grant a reasonable
continuance; and
WHEREAS, almost without exception, it will become known whether
either party desires a continuance during the time a matter is being prepared for
Masonic trial; and
WHEREAS, during the time of such preparation, the parties are pennitted
contact with the Trial Master, but not with the Commissioners, and arrangements
for a continuance can conveniently be made during that time with the Trial Master;
and

246

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

WHEREAS, pennitting a party the right to make a subsequent request for
a continuance directly to the Commissioners even if he has been turned down by
the Trial Master creates uncertainty as to whether a requested continuance will be
granted until the time the Commissioners actually convene and thereby creates the
possibility of unnecessarily inconveniencing witnesses or parties; and
WHEREAS, in state and federal court proceedings, the magistrate, as
opposed to the jury, detennines whetherrequests for continuances are t~ be grant~d,
and in Masonic trials, a Trial Master is generally equivalent to a magistrate while
the Commissioners are generally equivalent to a jury.
NOW, THEREFORE,BEITRESOLVEDthatSections32240and3233 0
of the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to eliminate all separate provisions
in the Masonic Code relating to the granting of a continuance request by either the
trail commissioners or the parties, and to provide that only the Trial Master shall
have the power to grant such a request.
Inasmuch as separate and different Sections dealing with the same subject
in our Masonic Code frequently leads to uncertainty and confusion, this
clarification is consistent with our Grand Lodge policy and general purposes.

ARTICL EV
THE TREASURER

Section 1. The Treasurer shall receive all monies from the
Secretary and shall keep an accurate and just account thereof.
He shall pay the same out only when an order is duly signed by
the Master, countersigned by the Secretary, and approved by
vote of the Lodge. He shall, at the Stated Meetings in August
and February of each year, submit a report in full ofthe monetary
expenditures, funds collected from the Secretary and assets of the
Lodge for the six month period ending on the preceding June 30
and the 12 month period ending on the preceding December 31
respectively. The Lodge may also at any time when considered
necessary cause him to present an account of his receipts and
disbursements, and the amount of funds on hand.
Section 2. He shall receive such compensation for his services
as the Lodge may direct.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 99-10 addresses the issue of compensation for the Lodge
treasurer. In 1988, legislation came before this Grand Lodge to pay the Grand
Treasurer. At that time, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes observed
that that office, like that of the Treasurer of the Lodge, was one of honor that did
not carry with it the necessity of compensation. The report went on to warn that the
passage of that legislation could ultimately lead to compensation for Masters and
Wardens for their work. That resolution did not pass.
Some Lodges already do compensate other officers. As such, this
legislation is consistent with our current policy. However, this legislation does
extend the policy of compensation to an additional officer.

§460. TRANSACTION OF BUSINESS.
Transaction of business in Grand Lodge at its Annual
Communications shall be upon written resolutions and reports.
All such resolutions must be presented to the Grand Secretary at
least 180 days prior to the commencement date of the next
Annual Communication. This restriction shall not apply to:
Decisions and recommendations of the Grand Master
A.
which are included in his written message presented at
the Annual Communication;
Emergent matters which may be presented and
B.

vote of the members present; and
Resolutions which form a part of the report of a
C.
committee and do not purport to amend the law of
Grand Lodge.
If a resolution is signed by two or more proponents, then there
must be stated the name or names of not more than two of the
proponents either of whom is authorized to represent and act for
the proponents with respect to the resolution before committees
and Grand Lodge.
Except as provided for elsewhere in this Code regarding the vote
required to amend the Constitution and Ordinances of Grand
Lodge, the transaction of business at its Annual Communication
shall be decided by a majority vote.
If resolutions of a similar nature on the same subject matter have
been presented to Grand Lodge at two consecutive Annual

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this resolution seek to change the voting percentages
whereby legislative changes to our California Masonic Code are made. Under our
current format, any proposal that receives a 5/6's vote is passed. However, any
proposal that receives a majority, but less than 5/6' s, of the vote is held over to the
next year; at that time, it can be passed by a 2/3 's vote. To many people, this would
appear to be a cumbersome process, in addition to being one that does not always
allow an immediate decision to be rendered. The proponents state that, in our
modem society, a•5/6's vote is almost impossible to obtain, and they suggest that
the process be simplified with the institution of a 2/3 'sup or down vote in the year
that the legislative change is presented.
The proponents are correct in the statement that a 5/6's vote is difficult to
obtain. This is not unique to modem society; it has always been that way. In fact,
it was for this very reason that the current system was put in place. In this way,
legislative changes that only reflect passions of the moment cannot be easily made.
The carryover provision actually allows a full year of more careful reflection on any
issue that obtained a simple majority vote.
The proponents seem to believe that a more rapid decision-making process
will result in better law. There is no evidence that this is the case. Instantaneous
gratification, in general, produces worse long-term outcomes.
The Annual Communications between 1994 and 1997 produced 23
Carryover pieces oflegislation; 11 of them received more than a2/3 's vote, but two
of them subsequently failed the next year. On the other hand, four of the 12 that
had received less than 2/3 ' s vote in the first year passed on the second attempt.
Hence, had the proposed rules been in place, a different outcome would have
. occurred for over 25% of the Carryover pieces. Of course, such a compilation does
not answer the important issue, namely which system would have produced better
results for the fraternity. However, your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes notes that one of the six with a different fate was Resolution 96-05, which

258

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

only received 59.5% the first year and, under the proposed system, would have been
rejected. That resolution received 67 .2% the next year and became law. Resolution
96-05 limited the proficiency to the obligation, signs, and modes ofrecognit ion.
This resolution appears to allow for more rapid, but not necessarily wiser,
passage or rejection of legislation. Since good legislation is not likely to go bad if
it is implemented a year later, the resolution, by eliminating important time for
reflection, is not consistent with our general purposes.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of the Resolution seek to correct outdated references and
clarify language in the California Masonic Code relating to Lodge investments. In
general, such a change is appropriate and consistent with our policies and purposes.
However, several of the changes that are being proposed do raise some technical
issues.
A requirement has been added that mandates the Lodge to confer and
counsel with a "Registered Investment Advisor" for any proposed investments.
There are numerous recognized Investment Advisors that are legally pennitted to
provide investment advice. This Resolution limits Lodge investment advice to a
"Registered Investment Advisor" only. The utilization of such an individual may
result in increased costs to the Lodge, ifthe Lodge previously relied on investment
advice from some other recognized advisor, such as the present Lodge Investment

Resolution No. 99-19
Requires Suspension of Member for Dues
Which Are Three Months Delinquent
The proponents of this Resolution seek to change the time for suspension for
nonpayment of dues from twelve to three months.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

GRAND LOOOE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

267

WHEREAS, Section 27070 of the California Masonic Code allows a
member twelve months of non-payment of dues before he may be suspended;
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge per capita is due and payable June 30th; and
WHEREAS, no other organization, fraternal or otherwise, allows a
member twelve months before he may be suspended.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 27070 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§27070. NON-PAYMENT OF DUES.
A member shall not be expelled from Masonry for non-payment
of dues, but may be suspended from all its rights and privileges.
In case any member has not paid his dues during a period ofH
1 months, and after notification by the Secretary, unless at the
next Stated Meeting either his dues are paid or sickness or
inability to pay is shown as the cause for the failure to pay, he
shall be declared by the Master to be suspended, unless for
special reasons shown, the Lodge shall remit his dues or grant
him further time for payment.
The Secretary shall give him notice of these requirements either
by registered letter or certified mail, with return receipt
requested, addressed to his last known address or by actual
service of notice, duly certified by the Tiler.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to change the time for suspension
for non-payment of dues from twelve to three months.
The payment of dues is a Mason's responsibility to help maintain a
Lodge's financial condition in a satisfactory manner. Many organizations will
suspend a member for non-payment of dues after a short period of time, but we as
Masons are honor bound to help a brother Mason if at all possible. A brother may
find himself in a precarious situation that would not allow him to pay his dues. A
three month period of time may not allow a Lodge enough timeto determine why
a brother has not paid his dues. This could also result in members not paying their
dues until after the per capita established by Grand Lodge has been assessed on a
Lodge based upon membership. The delinquent members could then pay their dues
in full and become members in good standing and the Lodge would not have to pay
the per capita established by Grand Lodge on these members.
This Resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of
Grand Lodge.

Resolution NOT ADOPTED.
