Resolution No. 99-22
Requires a Certain Design of the American Flag to Be Used by Lodges

To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M of California:
WHEREAS, the standard of the Continental Anny as ordered and carried
by Brothe~ General George Washington and his Anny was composed of the colors
of red, white and blue;
WHEREAS, !he flag <;>fthe United States of America. as established by the
Congress, was to cons 1st of stripes of red and white and white stars in a blue field·
WHE~AS, as Americans, we pledge allegiance to the flag of the United
States !lf Amenca and not to the banner of the United States, the trim or border
rendenng the flag a banner;
.
WHEREAS, the gold trim or border is but a variation ofthe color''yellow"
which color has a connotation of cowardice; and
WHEREAS, the hundreds ofthousands ofAmericans who have fought and

270

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

bled for the red, white and blue of America's flag are certainly not guilty of
cowardice.
NOW, THEREFOR E, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 16100 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

§16100. DlSPLA Y OF FLAG.
The Flag of our country shall be displayed at all meetings of
Lodges and carried on all ceremonial occasions except at
funerals. At the annual election of officers, and at such other
meetings as may be deemed desirable by the Master, the Flag
shall be formally presented at the altar and received in the
manner prescribed by the Grand Lecturer. Such Flag shall be in
the style adopted by the Congress of the United States only and
shall not be adorned with braid or trim.
The Altar of a Lodge shall not be decorated with any flag.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend our Code, regarding the
display of the Flag of our Country, to prohibit the use ofbraid or trim to adorn it.
They specifically refer to the "gold" or yellow fringe commonly used for this
purpose as having a connotation of cowardice, and that the "hundreds of thousands
of Americans who have fought and bled for the red, white and blue of America's
flag" are certainly not guilty of cowardice.
However, the Congressiona l Research Service of the Library of Congress,
in a paper entitled "The United States Flag" Pertinent Statutes and Regulations;
Selected Questions and Answers Regarding Proper Display of the Flag (the Federal
Flag Code); Recent Judicial Actions", dated January 8, 1973, had the following to
say regarding the use of fringe:
"The placing of a fringe on the flag is optional with the person or
organi:zation and no Act of Congress or executive Order either requires or prohibits
the practice, according to the Institute of Heraldry. It is not customary, however,
to display a flag with a fringe on it outdoors; indoor display of a fringed flag is in
accord with custom. The fringe on a flag is considered an "honorable enrichment
only" and its official use by the Army dates from 1895. A 1925 Attorney General's
Opinion (34 Op. Gen. 483) states, 'the fringe does not appear to be regarded as an
integral part of the flag, and its presence cannot be said to constitute an
unauthorized addition to the design prescribed by statute. An external fringe is to
be distinguished from letters, words or emblematic designs printed or superimposed
upon the body of the flag itself. Under the law such additions might be open to
objection as unauthorized ; but the same is not necessarily true of the fringe.'"
The absence of any Masonic laws, rules or regulations, to our knowledge,
on the question of use of fringe, indicates to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes that whether or not to display a flag with fringe or without it, wasleft to
the discretion of the person or organi:zation displaying the flag. Therefore, the
current policy being not to either require or prohibit the use of fringe on flags
displayed by Masonic organi:zations, this Resolution is not consistent with current
Grand Lodge policy.

§28060. HIRAM FOUNDATION.
The Grand Lodge of California recognizes the Hiram Foundation
Incorporated. a California nonprofit public benefit corporation,
formed on July 20, 1998. as a self-funded charity operated for the
purpose of providing emergency disaster relief to Masons and
their families. No Grand Lodge funds may be used to support
the operations of the Hiram Foundation Incorporated . However.
Lodges of this Jurisdiction and their members may be solicited
for support of those programs of the Hiram Foundation
Incorporated which provide emergency disaster relief to Masons
and their families. Such relief may be given to members of
Lodges of this Jurisdiction and members of Lodges under Grand

272

GRAND LOOOE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Lodges recognized by the Grand Lodge of California who reside
in California. Relief may also be given to California members
residing in other jurisdictions. Lodges are authorized to receive
applications for such relief.
For purposes of this program. a disaster is defined as any
interruption in nonnal living conditions due to accident or natural
causes such as fire. flood. earthquake, hurricane. tornado, acts of
violence or terrorism or any other similar event. It is not
necessary to wait for a declaration of disaster by a governmental
agency in order to render assistance.
Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
About two years ago, a California Mason became aware of the plight of
another Mason who had suffered from a disaster and needed immediate support to
get him through the first few weeks. Unfortunately, no relief was so available from
a variety of Masonic sources. Although that problem was ultimately resolved, this
California Mason realized that there was no avenue for the prompt provision of
housing, clothing, or other necessities to individual Masons who suffer calamitous
loss. In order to make such relief available, a charitable corporation was
established, the Hiram Foundation Incorporated. However, in order for this
Foundation to solicit financial support from California Masons and Lodges, it must
have official Grand Lodge recognition. The proponents are thus presenting this
legislation.
There does appear to be a need for such a mechanism to provide timely
assistance to Masons who, through no fault of their own, suddenly find themselves
in need of funds for food and shelter. Section 21080N of the CMC does allow
lodges to assist other lodges in times of disaster, but this regulation does not apply
to individual Masons.
An obvious concern that does need to be addressed is the effect that such
solicitation will have on other Masonic charities, such as the Masonic Homes, the
Masonic Foundation, and the Masonic Temple Association. Certainly, charitable
donations by any individual or lodge are going to be limited, and once money is
given to one worthy cause, it cannot also be provided elsewhere. However, we
already have an experience with this issue. As California Masonry has ventured
into each of its charitable activities, the previously established charities have had
to deal with the problem of potential reductions in their incomes. Nonetheless,
these other worthy activities have survivedand prospered in spite of competition.
The Masonic Homes remained in a satisfactory financial state after the emergence
of the Masonic Foundation. Similarly, the scholarship activities of the Foundation
have not been seriously impaired by the development of the Masonic Student
Assistance Training Program. History has taught us that the expansion of Masonic
charitable activity does more good than harm.
Since charity is a cornerstone of Masonry, this resolution is consistent with
Grand Lodge policies and purposes. However, unlike the aforementioned
recognized Masonic organizations, there is no apparent mechanism whereby Grand
Lodge will have any interaction in the management of the Hiram Foundation
Incorporated.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of Resolution No. 99-27 seek to change the installation
ritual as it applies to one of the ancient charges which point out the duties of the
Master of the Lodge.
They state that the charge as currently written is not in harmony with the
original charge contained in Anderson's Constitution of 1723 yet they offer no
evidence that the language they seek was ever adopted as the original California
Ritual.
The current language has been the installation ritual since at least 1947.
The requirement that ritualistic changes be made only to "restore" it to the
way it was from time immemorial was abolished in 1995.
As was stated by our Grand Lecturer in 1995, "the ritual as we received
it has historically been changed from time to time by Grand Lodge. Each such
change has been a change away from the original ritual, and has reflected the needs
of the time in which the changes were made. Obsolete and meaningless language
leads to confusion in the Temple."
Since 1995, it has been the policy ofGrand Lodge to change ritual to make
it as free from ambiguity and confusion as possible. However, to address every
slight difference between the ancient Masonic writings and ritual, there would be
no end to the changes that make no difference in the intent of the ritual.
This Resolution is not consistent with Grand Lodge policy or general
purposes.

Resolution No. 99-28
Restricts Wearing of Head Covering to
Master of Lodge Only Except at Funerals
The proponents of this Resolution seek to restrict anyone from wearing head
coverings other than the Master, except at funerals.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
During the Masonic year of 1995-96, Grand Master Alexander ruled that
it was appropriate for Masons to weary!1111lulkes ~ addit~on to.apro~s _at the ~e!'ll
of a Jewish brother. The Ritual Committee took issue with th 1s decision, behevmg
that a head covering was not the appropriate character of any Mason except the
presiding officer. Nonetheless, the decision was approved at the 199~ Ann.ual
Communication. Two years later, a Jewish Mason wore a yarmulke dunng a tiled
session of his lodge. The question of head coverings was again raised. Grand
Master Wordlow decided that the yarmulke was being worn as a symbol of personal
religious devotiou, and nothing in our law prohibited i~. The Ritual ~omm.it!ee
disagreed. At last year's Communication, Most Worshipful Wordlow s dec1s1on
was not affinned.
The proponents of this resolution wish to codify a prohibition of head
coverings by anyone other than the officiant at any activity when aprons are worn
except at a funeral.
This committee has previously regarded the wearing of a yarmulke by a
Jewish brother as a sign of respect for the Supreme Being, not as an effort t~
confuse the identity of the presiding officer. The wearing of the yarmulke is
comparable to the wearing of a religious pin such as a cross, an activity that Masons
all accept, and many pract!ce, inside a tiled lod~e: To limit !he wearing of personal
religious artifacts to certam areas of the body 1s mappropnate.
There is an important consequence to the enactment of this resolution. As
part of their religious practice, some Jewish males believe that they must wear a
yarmulke throughout the entire day. This _Proh_ib_ition of headwear w~uld force
these men to choose either Masonry or their rehg1on, because the wearmg of the
yarmulke will deny them participation in Masonic activities. Excluding men from
Masonry because of their religious practices is clearly and completely contrary to
Masonic values and actions.
This committee does believe that those who choose to support this
.
legislation are doing so out of principle, not bec~us~ of any ~dverse feelings ~oward
a particular religious group. However, others withm and without the fraternity may

279

GRAND LODGE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

interpret this proposal as anti-Semitic in nature. As a group that promotes and
practices values such as tolerance, Masonry has to answer to a very high standard.
Masonry not only must avoid doing wrong, it must even avoid the appearance of
doing so. This resolution, if passed, will likely arouse an adverse reaction from
others. In fact, the large number of signers of the next resolution, 99-29, may be
a reflection of such a response.
For both philosophical and practical reasons, this resolution is not
consistent with the policies and purposes of the Grand Lodge of California.

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has noted the large
number of signatories to this resolution. It appears that an organized campaign was

matters are better resolved by the use of good judgment based on a close adherence
to our Masonic principles rather than by the more cumbersome legislative process.
This Resolution is not consistent with current Grand Lodge policy.

Resolution No. 99-29
Authorizes Members to Wear Yarmulkes
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow members to wear yarmulkes.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M o/California:

BE IT RESOLVED that there shall be no Constitution, Edict, Law, Rule
or Regulation of the Grand Lodge of California which shall prohibit or restrict the
wearing of a yarmulke by any candidate, Entered Apprentice, Fellowcraft or Master
Mason, which specifically includes any Master of a Lodge, Warden of a Lodge,
Treasurer of a Lodge, Secretary of a Lodge, any Appointed Officer of a Lodge and
any Visitor (whether a Mason or a non-Mason) at any tiled meeting of a Lodge or
this Grand Lodge, or at any open meeting, or at any Installation, or at any Masonic
Funeral, or at any Cornerstone Laying or at any event or meeting where the wearing
of Masonic aprons by a member is permitted. Furthermore, any pins or other
materials used by a candidate to secure his yarmulke to his head shall for the
purposes of our ritual be considered as a part of his person and not removable by
the candidate during the conferral of the degree.
Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

As this committee summarized the recent history of the yarmulke debate
in our report regarding Resolution 99-28, it will not be repeated at this time.
In both 1996 and 1998, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
noted that Section 380 of the CMC specifically prohibits Grand Lodge from
interfering or voicing an opinion with regard to religious matters. It is unfortunate
that Grand Lodge must continue to discuss legislation with religious overtones.
Presumably in response to the negative vote regarding Grand Master
Wordlow's Decision 3 last year, the proponents of this resolution seek to allow the
wearing of a yarmulke at any Masonic gathering. As was stated in this committees'
discussion of Resolution 99-28, the wearing of a yarmulke is analagous to the
wearing of any personal religious artifact and in keeping with our practices.
However, this resolution, by singling out the yarmulke instead of more generically
including all religious artifacts, would force the Grand Lodge ofCalifornia to create
a legal exclusion based on a religious practice, an act which is in conflict with
Section 380 of the CMC. As such, it is contrary to current policy.

§26090. APPLICATIONS.

Applications for the degrees and for affiliation shall be on the
form approved by Grand Lodge, si~ed by the applicant, or for
affiliation, by mark properly attested, if unable to write by reason
of physical affliction, and recommended by at least two members
of the Lodge. A recommender need not have previously known
the applicant, as long as prior to signing the afplication he first
makes a careful investigation to ascertain i the applicant is
worthy. Recommendation of an applicant is a personal pledge of
Masonic honor to the Lodge that the applicant possesses the
positive qualifications required. Any recommendation once
given cannot be withdrawn after the application has been
received by the Lodge. References need not be Masons or of the
male gender.
Applications for degrees shall not be received unless the portion
which is annexed to, and part of, the form prescribed has been
answered. An applicant may sign the completed application by
signature or by a mark attested to by two members of the Lodge.
An application is received when it is read by the Secretary at a
Stated Meeting, unless, by a majority vote, the Lodge declines to
receive it, which is equivalent to its withdrawal.
The Lodge cannot receive an application until the applicant has
attained the age of%+ J! years. The Master may not refuse to
receive an application or direct the Secretary to withhold it for
any other reason.
The refusal of a Lodge to receive an application is equivalent to
its withdrawal, and the ~plicant need not wait 12 months before
presenting another application to that or any other Lodge.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, the above named Lodges have very small memberships from
which to attract enough officers and members to provide a quorum for their stated
meetings;
WHEREAS, these Lodges are located in the higher snow laden areas of
the Sierra Nevada Mountain Range of California, making transportation often

WHEREAS, the membership of these Lodges are all

A Lodge shall hold a Stated Meeting for the transaction of its
regular business once in each calendar month, except that Lodges
whose By-Laws provide for meetings fixed by the phase of the
moon shall hold a Stated Meeting each lunar month. The

Board Meetings
Meetings of the Trustees are held on the first Wednesday of the month,
alternating between the Union City and Covina Homes.
The administrators and committee chainnen of the Board of Trustees
contribute in the preparation of this Annual Report as follows:

Staff in monitoring Admissions.
Over the past year and a half the adult facility at Covina has continued
with the expansion of Assisted Living services, resulting in the doubling ofAssisted
Living beds. And, in anticipation of the continued need for these services, the
entire facility has been licensed as Non-ambulatory.

Admissions Committee
by Victor Huward, Ph.D., and Ernest A. Pooleon, Co-Chairmen
The Admissions Review Program of the Board is a carefully developed
analysis and evaluation process that continues to be improved and refined to meet
the evolving needs of our Applicants, as well as the Homes Staff, and the Board
itself.
Over the past several years experience has confirmed the value of the
required overnight visit to one of the facilities by all applicants in order that
Administrators and Medical Staff can meet with them and evaluate them and assist
in determining the most appropriate placement. (The facility visited is not an
indication of where the most appropriate placement might be.) A report on this
overnight visit, together with the Medical Director's comments, is then added to the
information sent to Committee members.
Prior to the regular Board Meeting on the first Wednesday of each month,
the six Trustees who form the Admissions Committee (three from the North and
three from the South) have each received and carefully studied the applications for
Masonic assistance. Each Trustee reviews and evaluates the applications and
accompanying data. and then submits his comments and votes to the two cochainnen, who discuss the results of the vote by phone, and then present the results
at meetings of the entire Committee, at which time Homes Staff Representatives
and Administrators attend and assist in the discussion. The Committee's
recommendations are then presented to the full Board for final confirmation.
The Masonic Assistance Staff works closely with the Lodges and their
Secretaries to simplify the application process. Lodges no longer are required to
vote at a Stated Meeting to sponsor an application. However, Lodges are informed
of applications by members or widows oftheir members and can object if they so
wish.
The number of applications handled by the Committee for couples,
individuals and children continues to vary from month to month. Over the past
several years we have noted a decrease in the number of people applying for
Masonic Assistance, although we still have people on the waiting list.
The ongoing reconstruction at the Union City facility continues to require
close control of admissions. However, as room became available in the Assisted
Living-Ambulatory section, some admissions were accepted for this level of care.
And, as space permitted, a number of couples were admitted where one of the
members of the couple required Assisted Living Non-ambulatory or Skilled
Nursing level of care while the other member was capable of living at the
Independent Living level of care.
The Union City reconstruction has required both Staffand some Residents
to relocate to other areas of the campus to allow the work to proceed. This has
added to the need for close coordination between the Administrators and Assistance

Centennial Celebration Committee
by Jeff H. Eichner, Jr., Chairman
The Centennial Celebration Committee, consisting of Stanley M.
C!1Zfieaux, Alvin J. Weis, Kelly Wiest, Dale Ankney, Ronald Cooper and Jeff H.
Eichner, Jr., was charged with planning events and activities during 1998 to
celebrate the 10ot1i Anniversary of the Masonic Homes of California.
Many of the centennial events and activities were completed by July I,
1998, the start of this fiscal year. However, the largest and most significant event
of the centennial celebration took place this fiscal year. It was the rededication of
the Union City Home on Saturday, October I0, 1998, the culmination of the
committee's work.
About 1,000 people attended the rededication that started about 8:00 a.m.,
with coffee and donuts. After Grand Lodge was opened in the Siminoff Lodge
Room by Most Worshipful Anthony P. Wordlow, Grand Lodge Officers and
Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California gathered on the steps of Sim in off
Center for the rededication.
The rededication ceremonies were preceded by introductions of honored
guests by Kelly Wiest, Administrator of the Union City Home and host for the day,
musical selections by David Francis Philips, and remarks by the President of the
Masonic Homes·of California Board of Trustees, Stanley M. Cameaux, PGM.
After the rededication, the ceremonies concluded with Dale Ankney, Administrator
of the Covina Home, accepting proclamations and congratulatory letters from
Governor Pete Wilson, Secretary of State Bill Jones, the California State Assembly
and State Senate, and from the Mayor of the City Union City. Time capsule
displays, lunch and tours of the Home followed the ceremonies. It was a great day
to renew the Masonic Homes' commitment to "Building a Future Upon a Cenhuy

The Chainnan gratefully acknowledges the hard work, cooperation and
dedication ofthe committee, the dedication, hard work and initiative ofthe Masonic
Homes' staff, and the total support of the Board of Trustees in making the Masonic
Homes of California Centennial an event to remember.

The committee in 1999 consisted of the Chainnan; Right Worshipful
David C. Decker; Right Worshipful C. Ray Whitaker; Douglas A. Scott, CFO;
Kelly Wiest, Administrator - Union City; Dale Ankney, Administrator - Covina;
and Kira Reginato, Director of Masonic Assistance.
This years report consisted of an update of where we have been in the last
three years; a review of what other selected Masonic Homes in the United States
are providing; and recommendations for action to provide increased service to
eligible applicants.
Again this year, the committee expressed its concern for the continual
decline in applications and the reduced census in the adult areas of both Homes.
When the renovations are completed at Union city, the committee feels that we will
not be able to have sufficient applications to fill the apartments and has
recommended to the Board ofTrustees that a comprehensive survey and/or analysis
of the Fraternity's membership to determine the services/facilities they would
consider using, under what conditions, and if they would consider entering either
of the Homes. The results of this survey would be greatly beneficial to future
Boards of Trustees in guiding them to determine future building and policy
decisions along with community based services which might be provided. The
Board of Trustees accepted this recommendation and it is anticipated that a survey
of the members and widows will be completed this next Masonic Homes Fiscal
Year. After this survey is completed, more discussion on the application process,
the surrender of assets policy, and a potential for "fee for service" policy will
transpire. The survey should provide a base for determining why so many of the
brethren do not make application to the Home.
Work is continuing on alternative land use at the Union City Campus with
the regulating ageacies which include the City of Union City, the Alameda County
Water District, and the local Parks and Recreation District. The Masonic Homes
acquired an additional 35 acres north of the present facility for future use.
Again, the committee was concerned with the time which it takes for an
applicant to be admitted to the Home and the Board of Trustees adopted the
recommendation that the Lodges no longer be required to sponsor applications for
Masonic Assistance; however, the Lodges will still be required to assist with the
assignment of assets process and relocation of an applicant. This should shorten the
process by four weeks and should hasten the review of the applications.
The Board accepted recommendations to study a child care center at Union
City for both the employees of the Home and the community at large; a study to
determine if offering rehabilitation to the community in Union City and the
environs is a feasible idea; and to make the Masonic Home in Covina available to
a service provider for social day care to Masons and the community.
The Long Range Planning Committee continues to provide
recommendations which they feel will provide the care necessary for the elderly
and children in need at both the facilities in Covina and Union City.

Planned Giving Program
by Jeff H. Eichner, Jr., PM. Director ofCharitable Giving
The Planned Giving Program is charged with the responsibility of
providing information and assistance to people on how to make charitable gifts to
the Masonic Homes of California.
During the year information and assistance was provided to individuals,
fmancial advisors, and attorneys on various ways to make charitable gifts as direct
donations to the Masonic Homes of California or through some of the planned
giving options that provide donors with a lifetime income, a charitable tax
deduction, reducing estate taxes and avoidance of capital gains tax, if applicable.
Some of these charitable giving options include the Pooled Income Fund and
charitable remainder trusts.
The Masonic Homes ofCalifornia Pooled Income Fund offers an easy way
to make a charitable gift and receive benefits of a lifetime income, a charitable tax
deduction and avoidance of capital gains tax on appreciated securities held long
term. During the year $25,500 was added to existing Pooled Income Fund
accounts, three new accounts were established for $20,000, and $737,642 was
transferred to the Masonic Homes. As of June 30, I999, the Pooled Income Fund
had 68 participants with a year-end principal of $3,842,026 plus appreciation on
investments.
A charitable remainder trust allows an individual or couple to give assets
to the Masonic Homes of California without losing the income those assets might
generate during the donor's lifetime. One of the biggest advantages of charitable
remainder trusts is that they can be tailored so that the trust meets the individual's
needs. Once the trust is created by transferring either cash or assets, e.g.,
appreciated stocks, bonds, or real estate, the donor will choose a trustee(s}, income
beneficiaries and will determine what level ofincome the income beneficiaries want
to receive from the trust. Generally the charitable remainder trust will sell the
assets, avoiding all capital gains, and reinvest the,roceeds in a manner that will
provide the income beneficiaries with the level o income chosen. Donation of
highly appreciated but low-yielding investments usually results in the donor
receiving greater income from those assets. In addition, the donor receives a
charitable tax deduction.
Information and assistance was also provided throughout the year on
Wills. Making bequests in a Will is one of the most common and welcomed ways
to make a gift to the Masonic Homes.
Charitable giving through a living or family trust is another popular
method of making gifts to the Masonic Homes and informationabout the benefits
of such trusts was provided during the year. Some of the benefits of revocable and
irrevocable trusts mclude reducing or eliminating estate taxes, maintaining control
of an estate even during disability, maintaining control over distribution of assets,
and avoiding lengthy and costly probate. Living or family trusts can be used to
achieve both charitable and non-charitable objectives that can benefit the individual,
family members, and the Masonic Homes of California.

Policy Committee
by Charles H. Alexander, PGM, Chairman
The principal function of the Policy Committee is to prepare changes in
the Policy Manual when policies are amended or changed by the Board of Trustees.
1999 has seen only one significant policy change. Chapter IV, Policy
.007, Admission Policy was amended to more clearly state admission criteria for
applications to the Masonic Homes of California. This change was adopted by the
Board of Trustees at the regular meeting of April 7, 1999.
There are several policy changes under consideration, but which have not
yet been adopted. For example, there is a proposal to modify the prohibition
against any resident having an automobile. There have also beensome proposals
to liberalize the requirement of total assignment of assets. If and when these are
adopted, the Policy Committee will draft new policy statements for the approval of
the Board of Trustees.
One project should be undertaken without too much delay. It would be
advisable to reprint the entire Policy Manual and issue new copies. As various
changes have been made changes have resulted in pagination that, while not
serious, are sometime inconvenient to the user of the Policy Manual.

Real Estate Committee
by Victor Howard, PhD., Chairman
The Real Estate Committee ofthe Masonic Homes ofCalifornia is charged
with the responsibility of disposing of all real estate and automobiles made
available to the Masonic Homes through asset assignment, wills and bequests, gifts
and grants.
During the past fiscal year, July 1, 1998 through June 30, 1999, we sold
a total of nine pieces of property for a total of $1, 164,011. In addition, we sold
fourteen motor vehicles for a total of$22,875.
We reduced notes receivable by $217 ,823 during the year, and were left
with 23 notes and $806,517 in receivables at fiscal year end.
Due to the terms of the Life Care Contract signed by each new resident of
the Homes, we almost always have an inventory of unsold properties. This affords
the new residents a 90-day period to adjust and make up their own minds that they
have no intention of withdrawing from the Masonic Home. The resident then signs
a release authorizing the sale of their property.
The Real Estate Committee wishes to thank the Staff in San Francisco, the
Administrators of our two Homes, Mr Dale Ankney and Mr Kelly Wiest, and
particularly Brothers Tom McKinney and Doug Scott, and Mrs Betty Blidy, for
their continuing assistance and support in all of these transactions.

Report of the Administrator
Masonic Home, Union City
1998-1999

Once again, I have the privilege of submitting my annual report in the
capacity as Administrator of the Masonic Home for Adults.
Nineteen Hundred Ninety-Nine marks the first year in our second century
of caring. I ask you to think for a moment about this statement. Long before we
had a facility, we had a tradition of men with vision who believed in helping others
and dreamed of how they could make a difference. Today, we can look with great
pride at the progress California Masons have made during the past century.
Since our inception more than a century ago, California Masons have
worked together to improve the quality of lifefor those served at this great home.
In preparing for the new millennium, on August l, 1998, the Trusteesof
the Masonic Homes of California adopted the following New Mission Statement:
"To provide quality care to adults and children, with dignity and
compassion, within an atmosphere, based on Masonic tenets, that fulfills
the physical, social, spiritual and nurturing needs of our extended
community."
If you have ever visited either this Home or the Covina Home, I am sure
you will agree that both Homes exemplify this Mission Statement.
11
In its l 01 year since it began serving retired Masons and their wives or
widows, the Masonic Home for Adults at Union City is preparing its multi-building
community located on 267 acres to serve the fraternity well into the next
millennium. As a licensed Continuing Care Retirement Community, the Masonic
Home for Adults offers three levels of care: Independent, Assisted Living and
Skilled Nursing.

This is an ideal setting for single seniors who want the security of all
medical care being provided on one campus, except for acute care, which is
provided by local hospitals. It is especially appealing to married couples who may
require different levels of care. In other locations, sometimes couples must live
apart and possibly in different communities. But at Union City, couples always
remain on our campus and if they have a medical need for differing levels of care,
visits between spaces can be easily made.
Since 1995, three major buildings (Adams, Wollenberg and North Wing)
have been totally renovated with extensive earthquake retrofitting, electrical and
plumbing upgrades, and the installation of air conditioning. Apartments that once
averaged 225 sq. ft. are now on average 450 to 490 sq. ft. and have private
telephones, personal computer access, individual kitchenettes, and in-room
thermostats for resident control of air conditioning and heating.
The South Wing residence is currently under renovation. When completed
in February 2001, it will return with 12 studio apartments and 28 one bedroom
apartments, which average 544 sq. ft. Later this fall, the Main Administration
Building will also undergo renovation and is scheduled to reopen in July, 2001.
The Main Administration Building will once again house Administrative offices

298

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and resident apartments on the upper levels (7 studios and 24 one bedroom
apartments). These, too, will be wired for computers and telephones and the South
Wing apartments for independent residents will have kitchen stoves. Other recent
modern improvements are the Grider Health Center, located in the Wollenberg
Building, consisting of an indoor pool, spa, exercise gym and juice bar. In the
Adams Building there is a modern spacious Ceramics Room, Arts and Crafts Room,
Sewing Room, and Computer Learning Center, plus a small lounge area for
residents' private parties.
Amenities to be available in 200 I in the South Wing are a 20 seat Theater
In The Round, Bingo and Game Room, Clothing Center, and an Ice Cream Parlor
complete with an elevated model train.
All of these renovations will supplement our existing superb medical
services available to our residents: Skilled Nursing care in our 125 bed Lorber
Building with computerized medical records, Medical and Dental Clinics, in-house
Pharmacy, as well as a Specialty Suite in which medical specialists such as
optometry, podiatry, neurology, dermatology, chiropractic and audiology are on-site
services.
The most notable achievement of this past year was the Centennial
rededication ceremony held on the Home's grounds on Saturday, October 10, 1998.
Grand Lodge officers under the direction of Grand Master Anthony P. Wordlow
conducted this sr:cial ceremony, which was attended by more than l ,000 people.
The October 10 date is just two days short of one hundred years ago when the
Home was originally dedicated.
For future Masonic generations to note; the contents of the 1896
Cornerstone casket which were outlined in the Administrator's Centennial year
report 1997-1998, were reinterred behind the original 24" x 24" cornerstone dated
October 14, 1896; except for the engraved plate, which was not found in the casket.
The new Centennial red brick monument, located to the left of the
SiminoffCenter and erected in 1998, hopefully to be opened and examined at our
bicentennial celebration in the year 2098 contains the following items:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

Report of the Administrator
Masonic Homes, Covina
1998-99

In addition to establishing our own educational arm to provide a better
means of administering our child care model, we worked tirelessly throughout the
past year in designing new homes for our children. One very important element of
the Family Home Model that we have been unable to accommodate in our current
cottage configuration is that of child meal preparation and in-home dining. Our
research has clearly indicated that the most meaningful interchange that takes place
within a family is during meal preparation and at the dining room table.
Unfortunately, because our existing cottages were never designed to allow for inhome meal preparation, this important element of our care model has been lacking.
This situation, in combination with the fact that our cottages are in need of major
renovation, led us to conclude that it would be in the best interests of our program
to raze the existing cottages and construct new homes. Working with a local
architect, our child care staff and Boys Town consultants have designed several
new homes that will soon replace most of our existing cottages. The razing and
construction is due to begin later during 1999 with completion of six homes
scheduled by the end of2000. Needless to say, the children and staff are excited
about their new community which, when completed, will allow for the full
implementation of the Family Home Model of Care.
Finally, with regard to our children's program, a number of steps were
taken outside our primary care model to improve our children's chances for success
upon leaving the Home. Although we have employed the services oftwo clinical
psychologists for many years, as our census of children has grown and the
children's needs increased, we felt some additional support in this area was
appropriate. As a result, we have arranged with Azusa Pacific College for graduate
students in the Marriage and Family counseling program to serve their residencies
on our campus. Under the direction of our clinical psychologists, these graduate
students conduct therapy sessions with our children in such areas as grief therapy,
anger management and adjustment therapy. By assuming responsibility for these
therapeutic interventions, our clinical psychologists can devote more of their time
to our children who are in need of intensive therapy. This arrangement not only
better serves the needs of our children, but it acquaints the greater educational
establishment and outside communitywith the commitment our Fraternity has made
to the children of our jurisdiction.
Likewise, we have taken extraordinary steps in seeing that our children
reach their fullest academic potential. Many of our children come to us with
serious academic deficiencies which require immediate attention. Working with
experts who are familiar with these deficiencies, our child care staff is challenging
local school authorities to commit the necessary resources to allow our children to
regain lost academic ground. Individualized education plans are now being
implemented when the child begins exhibiting learning deficiencies, not at some
unspecified later date. And when it is determined that one of our children can only
regain ground in a special academic setting, immediate steps are taken to identify
and enroll that child in the appropriate program, always with the intention of mainstreaming the child back into the public school when the deficiencies are overcome.
With the advent of the new millennium, an "Academic Success 2000" program will
also be implemented at our Home which will help ensure that our children will
receive all of the tutoring, academic assistance, and staff time necessary to be
successful in school, no matter what their innate capabilities may be.

It is with pleasure and great pride that I write the final ~nual report of the
current millennium to the Fraternity. As has been the case with so many ~eports
previous to this one, l am happy to report that because of your .generosity '.lfld
support, the Masonic Home at Covina continues to prosper and provide outstandmg
care to those in need.
In each of the previous four years I have made it a practice to characterize
the year so you might.better unde~tand the basic. nature .of that year's work at our
Home. And this year is no exception to that practice. This most current year would
best be described as one of refmement and growth.
As you will learn in more detail later in this report, the refinements to
which I refer took place in both our children and adult programs. The refmements
were made necessary not only because of the changing nature of our clientele, .but
because of changing governmental regulations and the ove~ll growth of our chent
base. Most importantly, the changes we have made c~ntmue to pl~e.us on. the
forefront of care delivery to those who reside at the Covma Home. This is not Just
my opinion, it is the consensus opinion of our industry counterparts as well as the
oversight bodies to which we are held accountable.
During this past year our child care program ~ontinued its march toward
preeminence in its field. You may recall from my previous reports that for the past
three years our Covina Home has e!Dployed. the servi~es of the Bors Town
organiz.ation for the purpose of educatmg staff m the practice ~fthe Fam_11Y Hom.e

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

Refinement and growth were the operative words on the adult side of our
campus as well. The adult community celebrates its tenth anniversary of operation
in January, 2000, and during its short existence, the care-giving effort at Covina has
developed far beyond that originally imagined.
The average age of a resident at Covina is 86 years, and to date, l 53
residents have called the Covina campus their home. It is not just good luck that
the average age of a resident on campus is 86 years. During the past four years our
care-giving efforts have expanded to include assisted living and hospice care. As
a result, when residents transition into these higher levels of care, it is no longer
necessary for them to transfer to other facilities. Often a resident simply stays in
his original apartment and our staffing is revised in line with the resident's
increasing health care needs. This concept of care is greatly appreciated by those
who live here and is especially appreciated by the residents' families who now may
stay near their loved one as he or she transitions through the continuum of care.
In order to strengthen our ability to provide higher levels of care, the
Covina campus is now undergoing a revision to its physical plant. As mentioned
in last year's report, the Board of Trustees approved our recommendation to
construct a new health services building central to the adult community which will
house health related functions in addition to a dining complex and various activities
centers. The planning and design work for that building took place during the past
year, and as of this writing we are breaking ground for the new building. If all goes
well, the building should be completed during late summer, 2000, and in full
operation immediately thereafter. Completion of the new health facility will permit
us to serve an even greater number of assisted living residents, thereby reducing
even further the need to transfer residents to other facilities.
Very similar to some.ofthe work we are doing on the children's side of
our campus to acquaint the greater public with our Fraternity• s Homes, in this past
year we established associations with several community agencies. Building upon
our existing relationship with Mt. San Antonio Community College, the Masonic
Home at Covina became a satellite facility for the college. The classes conducted
on our campus are geared to the Senior population and include our own residents
as well as individuals in the surrounding community. Specific classes conducted
on our campus include water color painting, current events discussions and mind
stretcher exercises. During the coming year it is our plan to begin an intergenerational class that will include young people outside our Home who are
interested in learning from the experiences of our Seniors.
In addition to our affiliation with Mt. San Antonio Community College,
the Covina Home has established a strong working relationship with the local
chapter of the Arthritis Foundation. During the summer months our pool facility
is used by the Foundation to conduct their "Twinges and Hinges" water aerobics
classes for Seniors. Three times per week our Seniors and many Seniors from the
local community gather for an hour of water exercise and general fun. Everyone
benefits from the experience, and once again, the greater community learns about
the wonderful nature of our Masonic family.
As I hope you have gathered from this year's report, it has indeed been a
year of refinement and growth, but it has also been a year in which we have laid the
groundwork for an even better future. With the re-development projects slated for
both of our communities, the Masonic Home at Covina will continue to be a

premier provider to those we are designed to serve. On behalf of the residents who
live here and the employees who serve their needs, I want to thank you for your
continuing support. Your support has allowed us to become the envy of others in
our industry, and we who work and live here do not take that supportfor granted.
Please know that our commitment to serving the Fraternity's needs will continue
to grow so that future residents of our Home may benefit from this wonder we call
the Masonic Homes.
Respectfully submitted,
Dale Ankney, Administrator

REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWME NT BOARD

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers and Members of the Grand Lodge,
Brethren:

Date
05/13199
05113199
09/22/98

Name

319

Date
10/17198
03/10/99

This report is being presented to you with extremely mixed emotions. On
the one hand, I am very proud of the opportunity I have had over the past six years
to serve as your chairman of this important board. However, the time has come for
me to relinquish the reins, so II will regretfully submit this last annual report to you.
I am also sorry that this report does not contain all good news. The final numbers
from the campaign for the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund this last year show
mixed results. Bear with me while I give you some of the vital statistics that will
summari:ze the results of our labors.
Receipts to the Fund from wills and bequests were $1,957,585.94. That
is an encouraging number, and is just a little below the average for the past 10
years. It is good to know that many of our brethren remember the Homes in their
wills. Without that dedication the picture would be bleak. Other memorial and
miscellaneous gifts amounted to $8,245.55.
Over 31,000 of you contributed to the Fund, and the average gift received
was $30.20. That is a pretty good number and that average has increased pretty
steadily over the past 10 years. However, the average contribution per member of
Grand Lodge went down to only $9.95. Is it true that we can only afford less than
$10.00 each for our Homes? We should be striving for an average of $20.00 to
$25.00 per member. That is the least we should do.
The not-sp-good picture is what you and I and the other members of our
craft do on an annual basis, straight out of our pockets, to build the Endowment
Fund. Total contributions received from the brethren through the lodges, through
the United Way, or directly to the Grand Lodge office, totaled $947,504.89. This
is the first year in recent history that these direct contributions have been less than
one million dollars. In fact, the records in my files indicate that there has been a
steady decline since 1987, when contributions reached almost $1.5 million.
It will be easy to say that this decline is directly attributable to the decrease
in the membership of our fraternity, but we cannot be so complacent. The fact is
that, in 1987, over 50% of our brethren made a contribution to the Homes
Endowment Fund; this year that figure was down to just under 33%. Why is that?
Surely everyone recogni:zes that the cost to care for our brethren and their wives
goes up every year, at least commensurate with inflationary increases. Your
Endowment board members try very hard to communicate this need to all the
brethren, but they must work through you, you who are sitting in this auditorium
and who represent the leadership of your lodges. We need your cooperation to do
the job.
It is time now for the test. I know you have been adding up the above
numbers in your heads, so how many of you can tell me what the total is? I knew
you would be right- the total increase to the Endowment Fund for 1998-1999 was
$2.913.336.20. That is not a bad number, but I don't want you all to have to die to
make it happen.

I have had a wonderful experience these past years as Chainnan of this
Board. The men who have worked with me (and for you) have been some of the

I also want to tell you what a fantastic group of brothers you have representing you

words. Worshipful Brother Richard Pumerantz will be your Endowment Chamnan

Richard and the committee cannot do it all, however. I want to close this
final report by reminding you of what you must do to make the Endowment Fund
program a success.

Article 25140 Section F of the California Masonic Code;
Second, recognize the month of May as Homes Endowment Month and
conduct a special program;

Fourth, ensure that prompt submissions of funds and accurate records are
made on a regular basis;
Fifth, call on your Board representative for presentations and reports; and
Sixth, visit the Homes if at all possible, for degrees or other events.
That may sound like a big order, but it is not too much when you consider
that this program is the most significant avenue by which we can practice our
commitment to Brotherly Love and Relief.

thatmostbeautif ulofproposition s- "Andnowabideth Faith, Hope, Charity, these

REPORT OF THE DIRECTO RS OF
Noe HILL MASONIC MANAGE MENT, INC.
To ~he Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

"The Shared Vision Continues." As a preface to last year's report to you,
rs, your Nob Hill Board confinned that the Temple Board (owners
stockholde
our
of this Masonic Center) and Nob Hill (operators of this Masonic Center) enjoy the
power ofa shared vision mutually developed. That shared vision, briefly stated, is
to do everything necessary and required to prepare and maintain this Masonic
Center for another forty or more years of service to Freemasonry and the Masons
of California.
This, then, is the second annual report to incorporate that special working
relationship. And as you might expect, when two entities share acommon vision
it is nearly impossible to report upon the activities of one without including the
activities of the other. Each, almost without effort, contributes to the programs,
accomplishments and successes of the other, with the ultimate beneficiary
California Freemasonry. With that caveat I tender Nob Hill's annual report.
As President, and on behalf of the Board of Directors, I am pleased to
present the seventh annual operating report for Nob Hill Masonic Management, Inc.
(Nob Hill). Because Nob Hill is the one and only for-profit entity owned and
operated by Grand Lodge, its annual report is somewhat different in content and
scope. Nob Hill was established by this Grand Lodge to operate for-profit the
California Masonic Center's auditorium, parking garage, exhibit hall, conference
rooms and various rental properties under tenns of a lease with the California
Masonic Memorial Temple.
This report is for the fiscal year July l, 1998 through June 30, 1999, and
will include only briefreference to financials. Full, complete, detailed and audited
financials are provided together with all other Grand Lodge financial reports by the
Grand Treasurer and published in the annual Proceedings.
A year ago I reported on the extensive Fair-Wear and Tear Projects
undertaken to both promote profit generation and to enhance Freemasonry's public
image. Details were provided for fifteen projects, some completed and some
underway. To that list we have since added another five related projects:
New flooring for and re-painting of the Exhibit Hall
New flooring for the Exhibit Hall lobby and hallway connecting to the
Library-Museum
New flooring in all five parking level elevator lobbies
Re-paint the stucco exterior of the entire Masonic Center
Add large potted plants to the Main Entrance Lobby
These twenty projects cost hundreds of thousands of dollars and spentdown a considerable portion of Nob Hill's recent profits. This result was fully
expected, planned and provided for in Nob Hill's long-tenn business plan. As an
example, Nob Hill invested nearly $100,000 in revamping the lighting, painting,
reconfiguring the parking spaces and traffic flow, increasing handicap reserved
parking, updating signage and security on all five parking levels. This project

327

resulted in sixty additional parking spaces, which will provide l 00% return on
inyestment within ~o to three years. Over time, the increase in garage revenues

REPORT OF THE COMMIITE E ON
CHILD ID PROGRAM
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F.& A.M. ofCalifornia:

The Child ID Program was instituted in April 1998 with the purchase of
the first computer system by the California Masonic Foundation. Two additional
systems were acquired by October 1998 and three more systems were acquired in
1999. The committee's responsibility is to schedule and support local Lodges who
wish to participate at local county fairs, street fairs, festivals, malls and other
events. In addition the committee maintains the equipment.
This program has been extremely well received by the public and the
participating Lodges. Members of the fraternity are very enthusiastic about the
program because it provides them with the opportunity to become known in their
communities and they receive positive feedback from parents about the work we
are doing for their children. It has been noted that some parents make it a point to
visit our booths in subsequent years after they have had their children photographed
and fingerprinted.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON INVESTMENT
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M ofCalifornia:

The Homes' Board of Trustees, through the Grand Lodge Investment
Committee, is responsible for managingthe investment process in a prudent manner
with regard to preserving the purchasing power of the principal while providing an
adequate reasonable total return to fund the Homes' future needs. In carrying out
these duties, Grand Lodge Investment Committee will retain a qualified investment
management consultant to assist in managing the assets of the funds. The
consultant's role is to provide guidance to the Investment Committee on matters
pertaining to the asset allocation of each fund's assets, including investment policy
and selection of investment managers and to monitor each fund's performance and
compliance with the Grand Lodge Investment Policy. The Grand Lodge Investment
Committee has the authority to select and retain investment managers for the
purpose of carrying out the Investment Policy of Grand Lodge.
The Homes' Board of Trustees shall approve the investment policy and
guidelines for the policy's implementation in consultation with the Grand Lodge
Investment Committee and the Grand Treasurer.
In order to fulfill our responsibilities in accordance with the Grand Lod~e
Investment Policy and Philosophy, the Investment Committee meets quarterly with
our Investment Consultant and Investment Managers. We review their respective
performances in conjunction with their asset allocation, compared to various indices
closely representing their objective. This process provides your Investment
Committee with the necessary data to properly evaluate each investment manager
on a timely basis, and to observe if they are meeting, exceeding or falling behind
our investment performance expectations.
The Investment Committee, with the guidance and advice of our
investment consultant has made significant progress in improving the performance
of the various portfolios of the Grand Lodge by implementing an asset allocation
policy that follows more traditional investment parameters for large non-profit

340

organiz.ations. Our assets are now widely diversified in large cap equities
value/growth, international equities, small cap equities - value, and fixed incomebonds and we continue to be alert to any additions or deletions that should be
considered that would add to our long term benefit, without undue risk to principal.
The market value of the total portfolio on August 31, 1999 was
$621,376,965 compared to $535,139,744 a year earlier, an increase of 16.1%.
Reference attachments that follow for a complete performance summary from
manager's inception by quarter and years.
Fiscal responsibility is the cornerstone of Freemasonry in California. Rest
assured that your investment committee is vigilant in pursuing the very best of our
established philosophy, policies and principles that pertain to the management of
Grand Lodge investments.
The accumulation of assets in the various funds of the Grand Lodge of
California have come about not only through the efforts of your Investment
Committee, but also from the contributions, generous bequests and continuing
efforts of Masons and their many friends. The operations of the Masonic Homes at
Union City and Covina are fmanced almost entirely from the income from the
General and Endowment Fund investments. The accomplishments that have been
made in improving our Masonic Homes in recent years is a tribute to the
establishment of common goals and mutual cooperation of the Masonic Homes
Board and the Grand Lodge Investment Committee.
I appreciate the splendid assistance and support that we have received
from our Grand Treasurer, Thomas C. Holm, Chief Financial Officer, Douglas A.
Scott, and Masonic Homes Board President, Past Grand Master Stanley M.
Cazneaux. They have made a lasting and valuable impression upon this committee
as to its importance in meeting the current and future needs of our Masonic Homes,
and have been instrumental in our adopting policies that will not only endure but
are equally prudent.
My personal thanks to the Grand Lodge Investment Committee Members
for their dedication and devotion in the support extended to me durin~ this past year
as your Chairman. The many additional demands of special meetmgs, plus our
regular meetings, did not diminish your enthusiasm or responsiveness, for which
I am truly grateful. I am reminded that it is the great people of the Investment
Committee who work so diligently that ensures the success of our committee now
and in the future.
Special thanks go to James F. Leggate, Chris U. Patropulos, and Joe
Winchell who have served with distinction and are now leaving the Committee.
Finally, Richard K. Pumerantz a valuable and dedicated member for the
past year is leaving to become the Chairman of the Masonic Homes Endowment
Committee, we wish him the very best in his new position.
Respectfully submitted,

The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the Grand
Master and the legal adviser to Grand Lodge when in session. The committee
reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered at the next
Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry out the
intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments on the
legality of the Grand Master's decisions and dispensations and on the legal effect
of the proposed recommendations and resolutions.
After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.
In the committee's view, those of Grand Master Nahin's decisions and
dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion. In the
committee's view, the legislation mailed by the Grand Secretary on July 15th of this
year is sufficient to carry out the intent of the proponents, and the legislation
contained in Grand Master Nahin's recommendations which he will present in his
message is sufficient to carry out his intent. We believe that each piece of this
legislation has the legal effect set forth in it.
The legislation mailed by the Grand Secretary on July 15111 of this year and
the legislation contained in Grand Master Nahin's recommendations require no
separate motion because they are automatically before this Annual Communication.
The presiding officer will announce the vote required for passage of each item
before discussion begins. Any legislation which does not amend theCalifornia
Masonic Code or lhe Ritual requires a simple majority only for adoption. Any
amendment to the California Masonic Code or the Ritual must be adopted by a
five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment receives a simple majority but less
than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries over to the next Annual
Communication when only a two-thirds affirmative vote is required for adoption .
We thank the Grand Master for the opportunity which he has given us to
serve this year.
Respectfully submitted.
R. Stephen Doan, PGM, Chairman

ritual means contmues to grow. We can no longer allow our candidates to pass
through the degrees of Masonry without going though some kind of Masonic

need and is acting accordingly.

Most Worshipful Melville H. Nahin, the elected and appointed corps of officers,
and the staff of the Grand Lodge office in San Francisco. Recognition is also given
to those special Masons who give of their time to act as Officers of the Masonic
Service Bureaus. Last, and of course not least, this Committee extends its greatest
admiration and appreciation to those ten Master Masons who serve this Fraternity
as Executive Secretaries of their respective Service Bureaus.
Respectfully submitted,
Howard J. Dumont, Chairman

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F.& A.M ofCalifornia:

Membership on the committee is one that has caused considerable
confusion since the Grand Lodge roster was published. At the suggestion of Most
Worshipful Mel Nahin, I took the liberty of reducing the size of the Widows
Committee districts and of increasing the number of coordinators on the committee
to give the individual coordinators each a more workable region. The result of this
was twofold.
First, I managed to salvage many coordinators who were overwhelmed by
the size of their districts and returned them to duty with a more workable
assignment.
Second, however, I created a recruiting problem for myselfwhich I did not
need, as many of the coordinator positions were already vacant.
Despite this second item, however, and with the help of many of the
Inspectors, I did manage to recruit a large number of coordinators. Membership on
the committee went from twenty-three in November to fifty-one presently, and
while there are still nine regions vacant, I am optimistic that these will be filled in
time for our next Grand Lodge Roster publication. 1 trust this has not been an
inconvenience to the Grand Lodge staff, and will continue this effort, if I receive
the approval of the Grand Master.
Grand Master's Itineraries have been the subject of several inquiries from
members who would like to involve themselves in the activities of Grand Lodge,
which I encourage my coordinators to do. S@veral years ago there was an executive
decision at Grand Lodge to discontinue sending these items to the committee
members individually in order to reduce costs. I'd like to see the sending of
itineraries resumed, as this tends to make the coordinators feel more a part of the
activity of the organi:zation. I suggest this mailing be part of the Widows
Committee budget.
Budget over the years has been reduced continually, owing to the reduced
income of Grand Lodge. I want to express my gratitude to the members of the
committee, for keeping expenditures down. I try to keep the regional meetings as
centralized as possible to minimize the costs to the members. In future, I will try
to travel to the various regions of the state to make personal contact with our
coordinators.
So far this year, only a very few of the brothers have found it necessary to
submit any expense vouchers, and those vouchers which were submitted were for
some rather unusual items the expenses for which were unavoidable and also quite
considerable. The usual and minor expenses have been pretty well ignored and
absorbed by our members, which has allowed us to stay well within budget, so far.
Sisters of Hiram Clubs. Fred Bryant, who was Chairman of the Widows
Committee a few years back, has been the person who has taken the responsibility
for coordinating Sisters of Hiram Clubs. The clubs have existed for over twentyfive years, but it has only been since 1991 that Grand Lodge has recognized them.
These clubs are now being sanctioned and encouraged by Grand Lodge, and may

Respectfully submitted,

• REPORT OF THE COMMITTE E ON
OFFICERS ' MANAGEM ENT WORKSHO PS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F.& A.M. of California:
The success of the current format allows us now to tum to the next step,
the standardization of the lesson plans. Such standar~ization will provi~e us with
a set of presentation topics for each in speakers' outlme form and also ID a short
prose document for distribution. As the program matures and becomes used and
organized by more and more people, such s~dar~izatio~ will provide a sound,
approved method of providing a set of teachlDg po1Dts with which any presenter
may convey the message.
Another outcome from our experience with the Workshops has ~en.the
obvious contradiction between presenting "basic" instruction of many topics ID a
short time interval and the desire of both participants and presenters to do a "full"
job oflearning and presenting the lesson plans. We will now begin using longer
presentation forums and therefore use fewer lesson plans for each Workshop. We
will cycle the lesson plans through three years.
Also, the participants will eventually learn that o.ur presenters mean what
they offer: that any Mason in California can call or e-mail our presenters and ask
them for in-depth help with their topics.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

Repetition of the Training Modules
Experience in education shows that repetition is key to learning. We have
intentionally chosen topics that can be repeated to the participants in both the
Officers' Management Workshops and in the Wardens' Leadership Retreats and be
classed into several "strands" of thought. Six such strands have been identified and
include: Masonic Education, Financial Management, Membership Development,
Program Development, Organizational Structure and Community Involvement.
Using a Masonic analogy, the introduction ofa topicat the Workshop is
seen as the creation of a rough ashlar in a quarry by an entered apprentice. This act
is a basic skill which creates a necessary building block for others to use creatively.
The principles of the use of these building blocks are taught to the Junior
Wardens at their Retreats. They are shown how the builder integrates the many
necessary building blocks to form a useful structure, or organization.
Using these building blocks creatively for the benefit of the Master's
specific Lodge is seen as the subject ofinstruction at the Senior Wardens' Retreats.
The Senior Warden is pictured as an architect who manipulates these basic building
blocks and the understanding of how they fit into a building to create a specific
building, or Lodge, which meets the needs of the members of the Lodge.

The Committee also served as the Grand Lodge representatives on the
Public Relations Oversight Committee and as consultants and advertising
representatives for the Grand Masters Public Relations Campaign. We assisted in
reviewing and hiring an Advertising and Public Relations firm, and overseeing and
implementing the campaign within the guidelines provided by the various
participating organizations.
The Committee assisted the Public Relations Oversight Committee in this
first year of the three year program by establishing guidelines for accurately
representing the obligations ofthe various organizations and began execution of the
program around the central theme "Something So Simple Isn't So Secret" in
Northern and Southern California newspapers, California distribution within
national news magazines and via distribution to all California Lodges. We
established a dedicated Toll Free phone number and web site for direct community
response and implemented a mechanism for responding to inquiries about
California Freemasonry, and referring these contacts to the Friend to Friend
Committee and local Lodges for additional contact. Approximately 80% of the
estimated Oversight Committee budget remains for years 2000 and 200 l.
In conclusion we would like to thank the Lodges throughout California for
their participation and support of the Grand Masters Public Relations Program and
to the many volunteers who have assisted in the campaign as well as serving their
local lodges public relations concerns. We appreciate the opportunity to serve the
members of the Grand Lodge. As my stewardship expires with this Annual
Communication, I would also like to thank the members of the Committee for their
support and active participation in our programs.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A.M ofCalifornia:
The Public Relations Committee functioned as the communications,
promotion and community recognition entity of the Grand Lodge. We wrote, and
distributed news releases, promotional announcements and advertising for various
Masonic events, such as Installations, Hiram and Golden Service Awards
presentations, Public Schools, Constitution and Friend to Friend programs, the Rose
Parade entry, Anniversaries, and community participation programs. We assisted

REPORT OF THE COMMIT IEE ON
RESEARC H AND PLANNIN G

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F.& A.M ofCalifornia:
Purpose
The Research and Planning Committee was named as a special committee
by Grand Master Melville H. Nahin, with the following purpose:

Conduct research, evaluate alternative s and make
recommendations on issues impacting Freemasonry in
California. Develop strategies and plans for consideration by
the Grand Lod$e, including a continuously updated frve year
strategic plan for this Jurisdiction.
Committe e goals and objectives:
Develop a meaningful strategic plan based on critical Masonic
issues, including Lodge improvement and societal relevance with
Grand Lodge support.
Recommend to the Grand Master for the 1999 Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge any appropriate changes to
theCMC.
Develop short term, immediate responses to concerns and/or
suggestions by the Grand Master.
Capitalize on and improve upon those activities currently
deemed successful while striving to minimize problems and
recommend actions considered high priority.
Recognize time and resource constraints and minimize
committee costs.
Committe e Results
The Committee met six times, five at the Masonic Home at Covina
immediately following the Homes Board meeting, effectively reducing cost and
spending under the budgeted amount. Considerable correspondence and other
communication has taken place between meetings among members of the
committee.
Assignments were given to and completed by individual committeemen
which provided research and recommendations for consideration by and action of
the Committee as a whole. A consensus was achieved for all recommendations and
publications of the Committee, which included all members of the progressive
elective line, the Grand Secretary and ChiefFinancial Officer, five Past Masters of
this Jurisdiction, two of whom are Past Grand Masters, and when named, the Jr.
Grand Warden designee.
The Committee has completed the task of defining and publishing a
strategic plan recognizing the critical issues facing the Fraternity in California,

GRAND LODGE F.& A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

359

building on the identified strengths to help minimize the problems. We also
suggested to the Grand Master specific recommendations for consideration by this
Grand Lodge.
Communic ation
The long term strategic plan developed by the Committee articulates a
vision and mission for Freemasonry in California. The Committee also identified
five strategic priorities, and identified several objectives and actions necessary to
achieve each strategic priority.
Communication with the Craft is vital. Prominently displayed during the
Annual Communication are the vision, mission and strategic priorities. These are
also included in the article, Optimistic Future for Freemasonry, in the autumn issue
of the California Freemason Magazine Another feature, California Masons
Looking Forward, will be included in the soon-to-be-published book to
commemorate the sesquicentennial of this Jurisdiction by the Masonic History
Committee.
The complete strategic plan has been published along with an abbreviated
version, a blueprint, Make A Difference. The Deputy Grand Master has arranged
for distribution to the Senior Warden of every Lodge and all District Inspectors, as
well as the Board Presidents and Committee Chairmen of this Grand Jurisdiction.
Copies are available from the Grand Secretaries office.
Conclusion
It is hoped that each Lodge will use the strategic plan to develop their own
goals and annual plans with help from Grand Lodge. Members of the Executive
Committee intend that the goals and operational plan for the Grand Lodge of
California along with the goals and annual plan for each Grand Lodge Board and
Grand Lodge Committee will be compatible with and further the implementation
of the strategic plan.
Thank you Grand Master Nahin for forming this committee and providing
us with your encouragement and support. We appreciate the opportunity to serve
the Craft.
Respectfully submitted,
E. Arthur Haglund, PGM, Chairman

REPOR T OF THE COMM ITIEE ON
SESQUICENTENNIAL CELEB RATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F.& A.M of California:

The SesquicenteMial Committee was reconstituted at the begiMing of the
Grand Lodge year and charged with the responsibility of planning for the l 501h
Anniversary Celebrations of our great Grand Lodge and to assist in stimulating
constituent lodges with plaMing events within their respective communities. With

Your committee has met formally on a monthly schedule throughout the
year and will continue to do so throughout our anniversary year. Individual and
sub-committee hours dedicated to the effort are measured in the hundreds. In my
many years of involvement in Grand Lodge Committees, I have never experienced
the dedication that the members of this committee have given in advancing this
effort.
Realizing the significance of this aMiversary, the committee established
a number of goals that needed to be addressed as part of the celebration year.
First and most importantly was the need to engage the constituent Lodges
in recognizing California Masonry in their own communities in concert
with events that would be held by the Grand Lodge.
We looked at planning for several major events that would focus on
drawing the public attention to the fraternity and its proud heritage in
California.
We believed that where profits may be generated, charities should be the
recipients.
We believed that commemoratives (aprons, etc.) should be part of the
celebrations.
We felt that the emphasis should be placed on highlighting Masonic
contributions to California's rich heritage.
We established that uniform images and messages should be developed to
identify the year and events.
To these ends, the committee has developed a number of programs, which
