Decorating Co., Pasadena, we selected a float design which honored the
Tournament of Roses for its long history of producing the outstanding spectacle of
the Rose Parade. The float design was based on the original Hunt Club horsedrawn carriage mounted on a 55 foot base. Several prominent celebrities associated
with the Rose Parade, space exploration, the entertainment industry and
Freemasonry were invited to ride on the float which was titled "A CENTURY OF
ROSES". The riders included Arthur D. Welsh, 1976 President of the Tournament
of Roses; Mrs Holly Halsted Balthis, 1930 Rose Parade Queen and granddaughter
ofamemberofPasade naLodgeNo.272; Dr. William Pickering,co-founde rofthe
Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena; Ms. Lee Meriwether, actress, former Miss
America in 1955 and former Grand Officer in California Rainbow for Girls; Brother
Norm Crosby, 33rd degree Mason and entertainer, and Most Worshipful Melville
H. Nahin, Grand Master of Masons in California. Our two Masonic representatives
were in the driver's seat on the carriage and "had charge" of the two model horses
on the float.
In addition to the celebrity riders, a rotating tri-visual panel at the rear of
the float displayed floral "portraits" of Holly Balthis as she appeared when she was
Rose Queen in 1930 and our Masonic brethren, John Glenn and John Wayne.
The decoration of the float was accomplished by 1177 decorators from the
youth groups and adults from various Masonic organiz.ations who donated a total
of7,150 hours to create this award winning float.
The cost of the float was approximately $132,000 which included the
$2,000 entry fee, $115,000 for the float contract and approximately $15,000 for
other expenses such as publicity flyers, fund raising appeals, food for the
decorators, office supplies, communications, riders' expenses, photography,
videography production, transportation, etc. Although this total cost was higher
than that of our previous floats, it was considered to be a prudent step toward
receiving an invitation to sponsor a float in the 2000 Parade for which there would
be very stiff competition.
The Family of Freemasonry was fortunate to be assigned a prominent
position in the Parade line up, being the 5th of the 56 floats. While this would
normally be a choice location, the major networks switched to commercials just as
our float passed the cameras. Other channels such as KTLA, Los Angeles,
Videospec, Home and Garden TV and Univision stayed with the Parade and
provided good coverage. The Committee produced a 15 minute video which
shows the construction and decoration of the float and its TV coverage during the
Parade.
Shortly after the 1999 Parade was completed, we received the coveted
invitation to sponsor a float in the 2000 Parade. We were overjoyed and relieved
to know that we had been accepted as one of the sponsors selected to participate in
the 2000 Parade. The theme of the 2000 Parade is "CELEBRATION 2000 VISIONS OF THE FUTURE". We immediately met with Phoenix Decorating Co.
to begin planning the 2000 float. There being no Masonic events to celebrate in the
year 2000, our attention was directed toward some design which would be readily
recognized by the public and which would enable us to convey some Masonic
message in a subtle manner. We finally settled on the Statue of Liberty as an
outstanding symbol of the freedoms which have been promoted by Freemasons for
centuries.

Phoenix envisioned a 40 foot high replica of the Statue of Liberty which
would have to collapse to a height of 17 feet to clear the freeway overpass near the
end of the Parade. We also agreed to have 80 small floral flags of countries from
which immigrants have entered the United States past this Statue. The negotiated
price for this float contract was $150,000, a fair price for this design when
compared with other spectacular floats of a similar type. With the $2,000 entry fee
and the other usual expenses, the total outlay is expected to be $165,000 for this
special occasion. The Committee and Phoenix also agreed that there was no need
for riders on this float as the float itself provides an important message. The Family
of Freemasonry sponsor identification will be prominently displayed above the
flags on each side of the float. The TV commentators have been furnished with
information about the role of French and American Freemasonry in the design,
construction, cornerstone and dedication ceremonies associated with the Statue.
During the design phase of the float contract, Phoenix felt that the height
of the Statue should be increased to 50 feet to improve its proportionality. This was
done at no additional expense. The Statue itself will be hinged at the point where
it rests on the pedestal and will be laid backwards to the horizontal position to clear
the freeway overpass.
Fund raising efforts are expected to produce sufficient income to meet the
costs of this float. The Committee wishes to thank Grand Master Melville H. Nahin
for sponsoring a Grand Master's pin program which was very successful this year.
As you are aware, the float program is conducted on a voluntary contribution basis
without the use of any per capita appropriation and its future depends on the support
of the fraternity at large. Each year, the Grand Lodges ofNorth America and other
appendant and concordant organiz.ations are provided with information about the
upcoming float and are invited to participate. Throughout the year, we have
received support from many of these organiz.ations but the combined contributions
from California Lodges and other organiz.ations is insufficient to sustain the
program without supplementary solicitations. Furthermore, it is necessary that the
supplemental funds be available in advance of the float contract so that we can be
assured of meeting our contractual obligations with the float builder.
The principal purpose of having a Freemason's float in the Rose Parade
is to stimulate interest in the fraternity and hopefully increase our membership. In
reviewing the I 998 Proceedings of the Grand Lodge, it is noted that there has been
a significant increase in Entered Apprentice, Fellowcraft and Master Mason degrees
conferred in 1998 for the first time in many years. In the absence of any other
identifiable reasons for these increases, the Float Committee is willing to accept the
credit for this promising turn of events.
The Committee wishes to acknowledge with appreciation the support of
many people and entities of the Grand Lodge - Grand Master Melville H. Nahin
and the Grand Lodge officers, the Grand Lodge office staff, the Masonic Home at
Covina for many courtesies and the use of the Home bus, Pasadena Scottish Rite
for hosting Committee meetings, Pasadena Lodge for youth accommodations and
hosting the New Year's Eve party for decorators, South Pasadena Lodge for youth
accommodations, Al Maiaikah Shrine RV Club for making their motor homes
available for the comfort of the riders prior to boarding the float, York Rite, Shrine
and Lodge members for cooking and serving food to the decoratorsand Southern
California Research Lodge for assistance in distributing float flyers to its members
throughout the world.

Finally, I want to express my deepest appreciation to the members of the
Committee who have worked tirelessly to ensure the success of each float. One of
the most dedicated members, Robert C. Coe, who has handled the bookkeeping and
accounting functions as well as many other tasks, has chosen to retire from the
Committee to enable him to carry out his other fraternal commitments. He and his
devoted wife, Saundra, have been pillars of strength for many years. The fraternity
owes them a strong expression of thanks for their services. On a sad note, in the
latter part of August, another of our dedicated Committeemen and tireless float
decorators, George Cronin, lost his left arm in a motor cycle accident on the
freeway. We sincerely regret his misfortune and wish him well in his rehabilitation.
It has been a pleasure and a privilege to serve the Grand Lodge and
Freemasonry in general in this worthwhileproject. We trust that our efforts meet
with your approval.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
TOWN HALL MEETINGS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F.& A.M o/California:
The Grand Master decided this year to implement a program of Masonic
Town Hall Meetings similar to those which were first utilized by the Grand Lodge
of New York. The express purpose of these meetings was to make sure that our
Grand Lodge was aware ofthe thoughts and ideas prevalent among the brethren and
the brethren were, in turn, acquainted with the operations of Grand Lodge.
Some fourteen such Town Hall Meetings were held in the state this Grand
Lodge year with the sites having been chosen with the thought in mind that,
utilizing the concept of a 50 mile radius with an approximate hour's drive, all but
a very few of the brethren of the Grand Lodge of California would be afforded the
opportunity to attend one of the scheduled Town Hall Meetings.
Each program began by having the Grand Master make a few opening or
introductory remarks and, thereafter, he and others designated by him, answered the
questions framed by the brethren in attendance at the meeting. They were asked to
put their questions on 5x8 cards which were made available at the registration table.
After a question was answered, follow-up questions or comments were elicited
from the floor concerning the subject addressed.
Because all Masons, including Entered Apprentices and Fellowcrafts, were
in attendance, questions concerning ritual were not permitted.

REPORT OF THE COMMIT TEE ON
U.S. CONSTIT UTION OBSERVANCE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

Constitution Observance activity seems to be breaking out all over as
reports of lodge activities streamed in following Observance events. The Grand
Master issued his Proclamation directing all constituent bodies to participate,
individually or collectively, in meaningful patriotic programs and observances.
This guidance was followed by a letter from the chairman identifying resources that
can be used in conducting such programs. Increasingly, the Internet has become
an abundant resource for Constitution Observance materials. Copies of the
Constitution, the Amendments and the actions of our nation's founding fathers in
drafting this great document are readily accessible on the Internet. The National
Archives and Records Administration website at www.nara.govis an abundant site
for gathering background and resource materials.
Several years ago, the committee had a windfall in garnering materials that
had been used in the Bicentennial Commemoration of the Constitution. Of
particular interest were the pocket Constitytion of the United States booklets.
Regrettably, this supply soon became depleted and other sources were explored.
It was found that Representatives to the U.S. Congress had access to the pocket
Constitution and could make them available in quantity at no charge. The
document is identified as Senate Document I 05-11 and is an updated version of the
Bicentennial Edition.
Reports of lodge activities included the ap~ce of public officials at
lodges to discuss the Constitution and related topics. Events usually included
dinners and patriotic entertainment. San Jose Lodge No. I0 featured a unique
program with members of the American Civil War Association in costume
discussing the great Constitutional crisis that divided our nation in a bitter Civil
War. Southern California Masons, under the leadership of Ted Alexander,

369

pres~nted scholarship awards to students at a special ceremony conducted at a

making similar presentations.
As always, the Constitution Observance event at Knott's Berry Farm,
involving a large number of lodges in the Southern California area, has the
reputation of being one of the most attended. Ceremonies include presentation of
the SO State Flags by Masonic youth, building the Flag by the National Sojourners,
a Masonic play with characters rerresenting the signers of the Constitution, a salute
to our Armed Forces and musica entertainment by one of the Southern California
High School bands. The replica of Independence Hall adds to the decorum of this
event. Our next Chairman, Gene Collins, will place continued emphasis on this
program inasmuch as he serves on the staff at Independence Hall. Many lodges
reported combined Observance programs involving other lodges and organizations.
Lest we forget the sacrifices that our Armed Forces have made to protect
freedom and preserve our Constitution, the committee urges all California lodges

from June 2000 through Veteran's Day 2003. Many of our lodges were involved
with the SOlh Anniversary of World War II and were enthusiastic about participating

participated in the 1999 U.S. Constitution Observance Ceremonies.

reduction in the number of Lodges attending. This is the first decline in attendance
in the I 0 years the Retreats have been in operation. We are now providing training
to only forty-four (44) percent of the Lodges in our Jurisdiction. At this time in our
Grand Lodge history it is extremely important that we have well trained leaders as
Masters of our Lodges. Please renew your commitment to sending your Wardens
to these excellent leadership training sessions.
The following is a breakdown of the Retreats:
Senior Warden Retreat, North - 88 Wardens and 57 ladies
March 12-14, 1999, San Ramon Marriott Hotel at Bishop Ranch
Senior Warden Retreat, South - 92 Wardens and 53 ladies
March 19-21, 1999, Crowne Plaz.a at LAX Airport
Junior Warden Retreat, South - 97 Wardens and 65 ladies
April 30-May 2, 1999, Crowne Plaz.a at LAX Airport
Junior Warden Retreat, North - 85 Wardens and 60 ladies
May 14-16, 1999, San Ramon Marriott Hotel at Bishop Ranch
The Senior Wardens' Retreats were under the direction of our Deputy
Grand Master, Alvin J. Weis, and his wife, Virginia. These Retreats were built
around Brother Weis' theme, "Living The Dream - Building A Better Tomorrow".
Leadership training was provided in the areas of"The Power to Create", "Positive
Interaction With the Communi ty", "Freemaso nry and Religion",
"Communications", "Public Relations in 2000", "The Master's Responsibilities and
Obligations", "Developing Lodge Leadership", "lfEnough People Care", "Friendto-Friend", "Planning a Sixty Minute Stated Meeting", and "The Gift". The ladies
participated in many of the above subjects with their husbands and in addition
covered subjects on "Grand Lodge Week", "Planning a Program", "Masonic
Charities", and the "George Washington Masonic Memorial". All of the above
training was reinforced with Team Building Exercises and Group Reports.
The Junior Wardens' Retreats were under the direction of our Senior
Grand Warden, David C. Decker, and his wife, Nancy. These Retreats were built
around Brother Decker's theme, "Freemasonry - Cornerstone of the New
Millennium". Subjects covered in these Retreats included, "In Search of
Excellence", "Discovering the Future", "Communications", "Planning Your Year
as Master'', "Developing a Lodge Budget", "Reviewing the Books of a Lodge",

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M o/California:
During the 1999 Masonic Year your Committee on Youth Orders
continued to actively engage in and improve fraternalism with our youth orders.
The committee attended the Job's Daughters Grand Council and NORCAL .
DeMolay convention in November, the Rainbow Grand Assembly in March, the
Job's Daughters Grand Bethel in June and the SOCAL DeMolay Conclave in
September. In January the annual MA YO meeting with the Grand Master,
Executive Committee, adult leaders of the Youth Orders and your chairman was
held. In addition members of the committee attended many area and local meetings
of the various Youth Orders. The committee also accepted the invitation of the
Officers Management Workshop to attend their sessions and provide information
on the youth orders.
The committee held three regular meetings in January, April, and August.
Committee deliberations and actions included:

During the NORCAL De Mo lay convention the NORCAL Jurisdiction Master
Councilor initiated and chaired a meeting of both youth and adult leaders from the
Youth Orders, the Deputy Grand Master, the chairman of this committee and
leaders of other Masonic bodies. The initial meeting was followed by a general
meeting of all the youth in attendance at the convention. Discussions at this
meeting were both provocative and productive and resulted in enthusiastic support
for follow-up meetings. Sub-committees were established to investigate possible
common activities for participation by all Youth Orders. Additional meetings were
held at Grand Assembly and the SOCAL DeMolay Convention. Common activities
held during the year were: a basketball tournament, and dances during Grand
Assembly, Grand Bethel and the SOCAL DeMolay Conclave. All youth leaders
were emphatic that the Youth Orders together with the other Masonic Bodies must
work as a family for renewal of the Fraternity.
